📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it’s Thanksgiving week and, for those of us who live and breathe the art market, that means only the briefest of breaks between the all-key November auction season and the year’s grand finale at Art Basel Miami Beach.
  • Sources indicate that perhaps more than in any other industry, the health of the art market is in the eye of the beholder.
  • According to data from ARTDAI, the November evening sales at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips generated $2.03 billion, a modest 7.5 percent increase over 2025, but the highest total since 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s Thanksgiving week and, for those of us who live and breathe the art market, that means only the briefest of breaks between the all-key November auction season and the year’s grand finale at Art Basel Miami Beach. But before we turn to Miami, a quick post-mortem on the marquee sales just passed.

Sources indicate that perhaps more than in any other industry, the health of the art market is in the eye of the beholder. Do you measure it by overall totals? By sell-through rate? By the number of bidders, or the number of guaranteed lots? By the ratio of hammer prices to estimates? Each figure tells a slightly different story, leaving plenty for our resident market whisperers to debate. But before we turn this week’s column over to the advisers, let’s set out some basic figures.

According to data from ARTDAI, the November evening sales at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips generated $2.03 billion, a modest 7.5 percent increase over 2025, but the highest total since 2022. Sotheby’s led the pack with $1.16 billion, clearing $1 billion and taking more than half of the three houses’ combined total for the second straight year. (Its share rose to 57 percent from 53 percent. Christie’s share dropped to 38 percent from 43 percent, while Phillips’s ticked up to 5 percent from 4 percent, pushed by the $44.6 million Modigliani sculpture.).

Recent findings suggest that and yes, the $384 million gap between Sotheby’s and Christie’s is roughly what the Blaquier-Arrieta collection brought in on its own: $412 million on just 12 lots. Winning those big consignments really does matter.

But for all those gaudy totals, there was a definite sense watching the week’s sales that bidding was uneven, thin, and at times absent entirely. Blame fickle collectors, sure, but it seems the auction houses pushed their estimates to the limit. Per ARTDAI, hammer prices across the various-owner sales in November 2025 came in 17 percent above the low estimates and at roughly 80 percent of the high estimates. This season, hammer prices for the same sales (i.e. excluding the Blaquier-Arrieta single-owner sale) were flat against the low estimates and just 69 percent of the highs. As Sotheby’s CEO Charles Stewart said after the Blaquier-Arrieta sale last week, “Our estimates weren’t shy.”.

But does an aggressive auction house make for a weak market? Or is this the same market we’ve seen for the last few cycles—one that is choosy, blue-chip and provenance-driven, and competitive for the right objects—just approached differently by the specialists? That’s what we asked the advisers, along with their takes on everything from the spread of guarantees to that $190 million van Gogh.

Answers have been edited for clarity and concision.

In a recent development, evan Beard, Beard & Co: Our having to repeatedly chase Impressionist and Modern Day Sale works well above the high estimates with a fairly low hit rate tells us that the “flight to safety” is more than just a tired cliché. Even second- and third-tier Impressionists performed very well.

It has been revealed that liz Sterling, Sterling | Teel Capital: The strong result for the Jeff Koons Bob-Tail [at Sotheby’s] was a pleasant reminder that no matter how highly orchestrated evening sales have become, there are still surprises. Equally, the results for the small Robert Ryman and Robert Rauschenberg from the Agnes Gund collection clearly demonstrate that there is still connoisseurship in the market.

Nina del Rio, del Rio | Byers: I have always believed the market is driven by the number of participants; more bidders = higher prices, more volatility, and less predictability. The current moment feels more predictable, safe, and tempered—which would signal fewer bidders. Estimates were full, reflecting strong performance over the past few seasons, and the buyers are still there for the majority of material, which is European Impressionism and modernism and American postwar abstraction, but there was less competition and flatter prices as a result.

However, I was surprised by the sober bidding on the truly rare material, which represented a singular (once-in-a-lifetime) opportunity for buyers. Monday evening after the Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary auction, I told ARTnews I was excited for the Blaquier sale on Wednesday because of the rarity and quality of the works; well, I was wrong that rarity would translate into bidder competition and runaway prices. The fact is, each work was priced at the top end of the artists’ (very mature) markets—leaving little room for price discovery, and bidding was thin and tempered as a result. Did buyers perceive these prices as the very top end of the market? Yes, I think so, which meant little to no competition for great works.

It has been revealed that maria Brito: Believe it or not, the moment that caught my attention happened in Stockholm, with the sale of Hilma af Klint’s Ser III No. 5. It hammered at 108 million Swedish kronor against a high estimate of 8 million, an extraordinary 13.5 times the estimate! Here is an artist whose importance to the history of abstraction has been celebrated by major museums for years, but whose market barely existed because so few of her abstract paintings ever became available. And suddenly collectors were fighting to pay nearly $13 million for one.

Recent findings suggest that we saw something similar with Aaron Douglas’s Harriet Tubman in Newly introduced York, which sparked a seven-minute bidding war involving eight bidders and sold for $14.48 million against a high estimate of $3.5 million. I think this tells us something fascinating about today’s market. There is enormous capital available for historically significant, genuinely rare works, particularly by artists whose contributions have been undervalued. Collectors are willing to reconsider established price hierarchies, and when they really want something, they’re not shy about spending.

Allan Schwartzman, Schwartzman&: For me, there were several standout points: the fever for hot young artists at auction has passed; Robert Rauschenberg remains the most important innovator of the last 75 years, and yet his market remains undeservedly quiet; and behind that, Gilbert & George are a crazy bargain; even though their work is photographic, they are unique and should be commanding the prices of the great painters of their generation.

According to recent reports, erica Samuels, Samuels Creative: Beyond prices, this week highlighted a distinct mood across the field. There is a strong sense of collegiality—advisors, dealers, and auction houses are actively working together to ensure success for their clients amid a generally sideways market. The market relies as much on goodwill as it does on capital, and both were evident this week. Despite broader tech and financial shifts, such as the Anthropic IPO, this remains a human-driven market centered on human-made art.

Recent findings suggest that danielle Forest Brandi, Beaumont Nathan: There were a few revealing moments for us, but among them was the spectacular result for Monet’s La Barque. The price of $6.9 million was, on the one hand, a surprising result for a work that measured only 2 by 3 inches, but on the other hand, a good case study for how collectors are behaving at the top end of the market. Looking at that alone, it’s perhaps an irrational result, but when you think about the rarity of the object, the story, and how good that picture will look on someone’s wall, i.e., styled alongside their Chinese porcelain collection and Nakashima furniture, it starts to make sense. That’s how collectors are thinking right now; it’s the beauty of the art market and what makes collecting different from other pursuits.

Industry observers note that evan Beard: Two key themes drove the high third-party guarantee rate this season: (1) Much of the material came from single-owner sales that carried house guarantees—Blaquier, Baum, Clive Davis, etc.—so the houses had to put the risk off on third parties. (2) Consignor expectations were elevated coming off a strong spring season, which pushed estimates to a level that the houses felt more comfortable locking in guarantees rather than risk a lot going unsold.

According to recent reports, guarantees are fundamental at this point. They’re a behavior tool to get an early bid from a buyer and a behavioral tool to give comfort to a consignor. Both sides still have the chance at upside. Guarantees are an vital lubricant.

It has been revealed that nina del Rio: Estimates were high across both auction houses, reflecting the past six years of consistent demand and solid performance—especially for European modernism and postwar American abstraction. The auction houses agree to full estimates to compete for consignments. My guess is that Christie’s was less willing to offer house guarantees which were not backed by irrevocable bids at the start of the consignment-getting season. And Sotheby’s had a bit more faith that they would find an IB [irrevocable bid] later in the process. In brief, I believe Sotheby’s appetite for risk—and possibly their confidence in the market—was a bit stronger this season.

Industry observers note that maria Brito: Sotheby’s just unveiled its biggest-ever week of fine art sales at $1.31 billion, which is extraordinary. But let’s look underneath those numbers. Almost a third of that total came from just 12 paintings in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, all guaranteed, and the majority hammered below their low estimates. Sotheby’s guaranteed 77 percent of its evening lots compared with 47 percent at Christie’s, suggesting a much more aggressive approach to securing major consignments. Guarantees are essential to attracting exceptional property, and third-party guarantors can absorb much of the risk. But a guaranteed sale tells us little about competitive demand. What interests me is how many collectors were willing to bid beyond the guaranteed price. The money is clearly there. The willingness to compete at any price is another matter.

Allan Schwartzman: The numbers speak for themselves; I don’t have any great insights here.

Erica Samuels: Each house has a different appetite for risk and adapts its strategy based on the specific estate or group of works. So I think comparing things side by side is tricky because it’s not apples to apples. While guaranteeing lots significantly affects outcome variations, there is clear demand right now for artists like Warhol (Flowers, Soup Can), Celmins, and Albers in postwar, as well as Tanguy, Kandinsky, and Monet in the modern.

Danielle Forest Brandi: The IB market is relatively saturated at the moment, and there is a lot of competition. To be in the game, you need to be quick, decisive, and on the inside track. Collectors are clearly enjoying the ability to gain a competitive advantage through the IB mechanism, and it shapes behavior enormously. We find that collectors who don’t get the IB early on may not bid without it. That said, this season demonstrated us that when the guarantees are set too high, it can take the energy out of the room and make it harder for works to inspire competitive bidding.

It has been revealed that evan Beard: Elevated estimates repel potential bids. Blaquier estimates crowded out potential bids. Most works get auctioned three times in a season: the auction between the houses for the material; the auction among potential guarantors; and, finally, the auction among the general public. The first two auctions erode the margin for the houses. Keeping estimates low while winning consignments is always a tricky dance.

Liz Sterling: I think a lot of works found their market this season regardless of where the presale estimate was set. Where presale estimates were overly aggressive, the auction houses worked hard to match reserves to bids and get works sold. Conversely, works that were conservatively estimated, such as the Aaron Douglas and Edward Hopper at Sotheby’s, saw competition and achieved prices well in excess of their presale estimates.

Industry observers note that nina del Rio: The markets for the high-profile works this season, which were largely European Impressionist and modern, and American Abstract Expressionist, are all relatively mature, and the top end of the artists’ prices have largely been realized. Couple this with full estimates (which the auction houses had to offer sellers to win the business) and it leaves little room for price discovery, even for the exceedingly rare Blaquier van Gogh. I believe this affected competition for the van Gogh, the entire Blaquier sale, and several other highlights across all the auction houses. However, I can’t help but wonder whether the last-minute claim on the van Gogh took other bidders out of the mix? Just a thought … and certainly not unique to me.

Maria Brito: I think we’re reading too much into the number of bidders. In 2022, when the global art market reached its second-highest level in history, Orchard with Cypresses from the Paul Allen collection sold for $117.2 million with exactly three bidders. This week’s van Gogh also attracted three bidders, but fetched $190.4 million, more than 60 percent above the previous record. I consider Châtaigniers en fleurs a substantially better painting. Yes, it hammered at $165 million, below Sotheby’s $180 million expectation, but that doesn’t make the result disappointing. We also cannot ignore the Nazi-era provenance controversy, settled barely a day before the auction. Whether it deterred potential bidders is impossible to know. At this level of the market, buyers have extraordinary financial resources, but they still have their own ideas about value.

Recent findings suggest that allan Schwartzman: It brought a huge price. There were few bids because the auction houses sometimes have to stretch to get headline material. Many works that are competitively offered sell on few bids because the auction houses have already conducted an auction between themselves to get those works. This does not necessarily reflect a thin market.

It has been revealed that erica Samuels: I enjoy the philosophical roundabout of auction house estimates. There are different categories: the attractive, come-hither estimate; the punchy estimate; the estimate right in line with the market. It’s pretty nuanced, and you have to be careful about reading too much into them. An estimate is not a price tag. It’s a range, a suggestion. And to a certain extent, there’s a part of the auction world you only understand if you’re out there seeing a lot of things. Some artworks couldn’t sell privately, so they come to auction to try a broader audience. They may not find a buyer at any estimate.

But let’s be honest, it’s quite thin at the top. $190 million is a lot of money for any buyer to spend. No wonder it sold to a very seasoned professional.

Danielle Forest Brandi: The discrepancy between headline prices and estimates was a defining feature of the week. In recent years, the houses drove down estimates in an effort to revive competition, but it seems that pricing has crept back up. The thinness we saw with bidding was more indicative of these ambitious estimates than the market overall.

Evan Beard: From 2020 to 2023, we were in a pretty intense risk-on speculation cycle where emerging contemporary was hot, so a lot of that material got flipped to auction. We’re in a risk-off cycle now. So very few emerging contemporary lots need to go to auction because they are easily accessible privately. The pendulum will swing back, albeit for a fresh group of hot young artists.

Nina del Rio: There was a lot of American postwar and contemporary material on the market last week, but few really great, major examples in the auctions. Rothko, de Kooning, Richter, Frankenthaler, and Stella (among others) were well represented with fully priced seven- and eight-figure examples, but nothing outstanding or market-making vs. the great European material on offer. (It is worth noting that women artists from the same postwar period performed better, but were still uneven—Kusama and Agnes Martin in particular.).

De Kooning and Rothko are interesting case studies. While de Kooning was well represented, especially by the 1975 oil from the Hedreen collection at Sotheby’s and the Whitney’s de Kooning at Christie’s, both were fully estimated, and neither had the potential to push the artist’s market. Four Rothko paintings on paper were offered last week; one very good example sold well above estimate, and the other three examples, which were arguably not as strong, sold below estimate or were unsold.

Maria Brito: The contemporary market is suffering from serious fatigue. There are simply too many artists, too much work being produced, and too much material circulating. Collectors have become desensitized and increasingly skeptical, particularly after watching so many artists’ prices rise dramatically and then collapse.

In a recent development, compare that with Impressionism and modern art, where the universe of historically established artists is considerably smaller and the supply of important works is finite. There’s a level of scarcity and historical validation that gives buyers confidence. Contemporary art is a much more crowded field, and there’s simply not enough demand to support everyone at the prices we’ve become accustomed to seeing.

In a recent development, of course, exceptional artists and exceptional works will continue to command extraordinary prices, but collectors are increasingly questioning what’s genuinely worth pursuing. And I think that’s healthy.

It has been revealed that allan Schwartzman: The fever for hot young artists at auction is over for now. This is for several reasons: prices for most young artists for whom there was hysterical (read: speculative) buying at auction could not and did not live up to such lofty numbers; a new generation of artists has not emerged for which the market has the same speculative appetite (and that’s a good thing); and sometimes the market for young artists is very different at auction than at the galleries that represent artists and develop those markets.

Erica Samuels: Collectors are looking for historical depth far more than in previous seasons. A new wave of younger collectors is definitely entering the market. They are educated, critical thinkers who ask great questions, which makes for an exciting path forward. They want collections that move across generations of artists, not just one moment.

According to recent reports, danielle Forest Brandi: With some exceptions, the contemporary offering across both houses this season felt a bit tired in [the] view [of myself and my colleagues at Beaumont Nathan], especially in comparison to the Impressionist and modern. The depth and cultural authority of blue-chip modernism seems to offer an assuring sense of solidity and substance that is perhaps universally needed right now. Of course, tastes change, the market moves on, and in time the contemporary world will come back as that market continues to recalibrate. But in the meantime, it seems to us that collectors are more interested in the past than the present.

Sources indicate that evan Beard: Anyone who tells you that Gen Z is driving the art market in any meaningful way is either misinformed or trying to sell you a dream. The market is driven by a group of private equity, hedge fund, real estate, and tech entrepreneurs in their 50s and 60s. It’s the usual suspects. And each newly introduced year a few new significant buyers enter the fray. New wealth grows up and ultimately buys art. But young collectors are not a major driver at auction at the moment. How many Gen Z collectors are on the ARTnews Top 200 collectors list? Or the Forbes 400 list? Or any list? Their day is coming, though. We’ve got some young risers we’re working with.

Nina del Rio: I would be guessing if I had an answer to this question. Here’s what I know: buyer access to great quality primary market material, while still difficult and often reserved for museums, is less difficult than in the past. I believe the younger collectors are buying great material from galleries (as they should). There is less great material by living artists at auction, and the speculation in that auction market has quieted considerably.

Maria Brito: I didn’t see clear evidence of a major generational shift this week, but the reality is that we rarely know who the ultimate buyers are. So much of the bidding happens through advisors, dealers, and telephone representatives. The auction houses know who’s behind those paddles. The rest of us are largely guessing. There’s certainly growing participation from younger collectors, but we should distinguish between buying a $20,000 print and bidding $100 million on a painting. Younger wealth is entering the market, but I haven’t seen compelling evidence from this week’s sales that it has fundamentally changed who’s buying at the very top.

Allan Schwartzman: I was not in the room to observe live bidding.

Danielle Forest Brandi: Impressionism was clearly the dominant category during the November sales, across different levels of the market. We are seeing a growing generation of collectors who are engaged with this area and other historical categories, seeking established blue-chip names or, the inverse, overlooked artists in history like the female Surrealists. Prices across many historical areas of the market have come down from where they once were, making accessible entry points for newer collectors who want to buy things that have substance and will hold up over time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Waugh Thistleton Architects.

UK studio Waugh Thistleton Architects is set to transform the Edwardian Westbrook Pavilion in Margate, UK, into an arts centre for British artist Tracey Emin with a cafe, public sauna and changing rooms.

“The project will bring a much-loved seafront building back into use, combining its original purpose with fresh spaces for art, culture and the local community,” said Waugh Thistleton Architects.

The studio recently won planning permission from the local council to convert the abandoned building, which Emin purchased in 2023, into a facility run by the Tracey Emin Foundation.

The project aims to return the building to its former use as a changing room for swimmers and as a tea room, when it originally opened in 1914.

“Originally opened in 1914, the building provided public changing facilities for sea-bathing and a tea room,” said the studio.

“Following storm damage in the Great North Sea Storm of 1953, subsequent alterations detracted from its original Edwardian character,” it continued.

“The renovated pavilion will accommodate artist studios, an art gallery, clubroom, cafe, sea-bathing changing facilities, a new sauna and refurbished public toilets, restoring its original role as a place for bathing and socialising by the sea.”.

Along with making the pavilion a building used by the public again, the studio aims to return the building’s core to its Edwardian look by removing later additions. It will also add glazed facades to the wings on either side of the central pavilion.

The building will be topped by a rooftop terrace, while a public toilet on the site will be renovated.

“The design draws on the proportions and character of the original building, removing later additions and reinstating lost features such as the historic belvederes which top the central tower structures,” remarked the studio.

“The beachfront facade will see a new glazing system and colonnade to each of the building’s wings, with a new sheltered archway forming a new seating terrace at the building’s heart,” it continued.

In a recent development, “The design seeks to reference the original architecture while providing contemporary needs of a public building. Where original features are references, these are distinguishable architecturally.”.

Recent findings suggest that emin is one of the UK’s best-known living artists. We recently produced a video of a landmark exhibition of her work at Tate Modern.

Recent projects by Waugh Thistleton Architects include intends for the “tallest mass timber office building in the US”.

Images courtesy of Waugh Thistleton Architects.

#114527. Industry News: What Is Internet Cinema?

Industry News: What Is Internet Cinema?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot, a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet.
  • During last June’s heat wave, I found myself standing outside an unassuming office building in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, baking in the sun’s glare.
  • Once inside, I wandered around the cool, unlit space, laughing at funny paintings and sculptures until it was time to find a spot on the floor for the screening.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot, a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet.

During last June’s heat wave, I found myself standing outside an unassuming office building in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, baking in the sun’s glare. The Gallery, a nomadic curatorial platform, had set up an exhibition, titled “WeWork (oralmoral)”, in one of the building’s vacant office spaces. In celebration of the show’s closing the curators were screening films, some of which fall into the category of what is being called “internet cinema,” a burgeoning movement, or method, that has been in the making since late 2020. Related Articles Using the Graphics of GTA, Sara Sadik Explores the Challenges France's Muslim Youth Face 'Desiring Machines' Dares Us to Imagine a Healthy Relationship with Technology.

Once inside, I wandered around the cool, unlit space, laughing at funny paintings and sculptures until it was time to find a spot on the floor for the screening. Someone in front of me was hastily scrawling the lineup of the screenings on paper with a black marker and passing them around as fast as he produced them. One passed back to me. The first film on the list was Zarina Nares’ I am going to die (this is my sign) (2025). The projector was fiddled with and a rectangle of white with a buffer symbol appeared on the blank wall in front of the seated crowd.

Sources indicate that A chorus of female voices rose up, all in some general distress, and while I couldn’t see these women, by the tone, I could tell they were speaking into a front-facing camera. The chorus cut out to a single voice, which spoke over dashcam footage of a car crash: “You’re having problems at work, your boyfriend broke up with you, your parents are mad at you, everything is going wrong, your car broke down – that is a good sign. Like, that is the very best sign.”What followed was a montage of TikTok videos featuring motivational advice. One video bled into another, linked by the formulaic hooks used by podcast bros, emotional car seat influencers, clips of celebrities’ acceptance speeches, athletes in interviews, or passionate pastors, all of which was set to music. One after another these TikToks reveal ‘the one thing that you need to learn’ in a high-speed carousel of intense emotion that feels increasingly forced as it becomes clear how many of these impassioned speeches are copies of one another.

“Internet cinema isn’t necessarily about the internet or its aesthetic but about its logic, how it functions and how it makes us feel,” Zarina Nares said in a phone call. On the process of making I am going to die, she added that “Clearly, I watched enough advice videos for too long that I kept getting more. Once you watch so many you see the formula behind them, whether it’s a certain cadence of speaking or certain music.”.

Internet cinema was first defined in a 2007 paper by Chuck Tryon titled “Upcoming Media Studies and the New Internet Cinema.” The technologies and formats that concerned Tryon —iPods and camera phones, software like Final Cut Pro, and home movies—are far dated, but his paper was prescient, having tapped into impulses and concerns that reflect contemporary internet cinema: a do-it-yourself ethos that blurs the line between amateur and artist; the popularization of “niche exhibition;” and a “self-reflexive style” that works “to call attention to the narrative codes and technological specs that shape cultural productions.”.

Contemporary internet cinema has its roots in the COVID-era, which saw an explosion of participation in internet culture and production, that often bled out into one particular place: Dimes Square, a patch of Manhattan where Chinatown and the Lower East Side meet.

In a recent development, one of the most memorable dramas that played out at the time was puppeteered by a then-anonymous internet figure who went by the name Angelicism01. This figure posted creeds about extinction on Substack, and gained infamy for growing a cult-like following among young women in Newly introduced York (who had never met him). With the help of various film makers, he made a three-hour long movie called Film01 which includes fast paced montages of memes, tweets, videos of natural disasters and terrorist attacks, alongside long scenes featuring the ‘it-girls’ he had recruited. Writer Madeline Cash described Film01 in the art publication Spike as “an unsophisticated collage of localized content that mimics, rather than intervenes or questions, our digital conditions,” which ultimately did nothing more than tap “into the scene’s libidinal narcissism.”Yet, with some distance, Film01 has proven to be a productive experiment. One of Angelicism01’s collaborators, the filmmaker Dana Dawud, found internet footage to splice into the film, created short edits that became a part of the larger film, and remotely directed certain sequences. Dawud would go on to launch Open Secret, an international screening series of internet cinema that has since played a large part in consolidating disconnected artists and practices under the term.At the same time that young women were running around Dimes Square at Angelicism01’s request, people were locked away at home with TikTok. More than ever, people around the world were subjecting themselves to hours and hours of scrolling on this relatively new video content platform.“When you’re doom scrolling, there is, technically speaking, no specific author to this montage that you’re watching. So, it’s as if you’re exposed to radical experimental cinema all the time by a completely cynical industrial apparatus,” remarked 0nty, the co-author of “Dialogues on CoreCore & the Contemporary Online Avant-Garde” during a Zoom interview also attended by his co-author Mischa Dols. “The question is, how do you even begin to think about this problem? And I think internet cinema is an answer,” 0nty said.0nty and Dols describe internet cinema as a method, rather than a genre or an aesthetic, which seeks to expose or comment on the way that the internet functions through editing found footage.It’s worth noting that some works under the umbrella of internet cinema do feature the production of new images. Dahlia Bloomstone’s 20,000 Tokens (2025) is a screen recording of the artist chatting with men and exposing herself on the webcam site Chaturbate (the video is spliced with a glitching 3D-rendering of a blonde avatar in a black void). For The Sight is a Wound (2024), Parham Ghalamdar filmed himself burning his own paintings, as a statement on how tthe seemingly endless documentation of the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza has made images useless. Yet the particular process of editing found footage is usually highlighted in definitions of internet cinema because this method represents the folk practice that preceded internet cinema: corecore.

Core, or rather, -core, is a suffix that denotes some kind of bundle of aesthetics and moods. Cottagecore, for example, is a reference to an image universe of milkmaid tops, galoshes, a straw basket full of wildflowers, a shingled cottage, butter made with wooden tools, but also, beyond images, a wish for simple, optimistic, pastoral life. But corecore emerged not as a specific aesthetic but as a way of making video content through editing together music, clips from movies, podcasts, and other TikToks.These videos are often melancholic ruminations of the deep and unrecognized suffering of young men, the terrible sublimity of being alone with your screen, an alienated awareness of hurtling towards extinction while scrolling on your parents’ sofa. Watching compilations of corecore I reminded me intensely of my time on Tumblr as a teenager.

It has been revealed that on Tumblr, the practice of posting and reblogging images, fragments of text, and GIFs under an “aesthetic” was a way of cultivating and nurturing a feeling: a world of images that created a visual language for all that we thought life could be. Painful, dramatic love; intensity chased by the doom of its own ephemerality; cold, beautiful suffering. In the pivot to video platforms, corecore takes that tendency to collect images and feelings and turns it into a form much more contained and shareable than a blog: the film.

Removed from the usual logics of personal branding and sponsorship deals, it became an exciting trend for those who take internet-based cultural production seriously. Corecore, as a mass movement of people making films on the same devices they watch them on, represented the realization of an old dream of experimental cinema: film as a truly collective practice.“Authorship gets really muddy, you have content creators and video artists making films on the same platforms. Dana [Dawud] has compared internet cinema to the way that SoundCloud functions, where people can steal your edit, steal your beat, steal a sample, and then it gets lost who put it online first, and that’s okay,” stated Edison Niebla Rodriguez, a curator who also creates video art with his wife, Dayana Matasheva, under the name Demon Lovers Inc. “Obviously, it’s kind of at odds with video art which is very hard for people to see because of the way that the art market functions.”.

That stated, video art has been a major inspiration for artists working in internet cinema. Arthur Jafa’s Love Is the Message, the Message Is Death (2016) in particular is often cited as a kind of totem of legitimacy for internet cinema. The film is a montage of civil rights–era footage and grainy videos of Black Americans circulated online: reaction memes, women twerking, women getting slammed to the ground by police, men getting shot by police, arms raised in the air. It’s profound love and profound despair, but also a comment on how images of Black people circulate online. When I first saw it, I was struck by how internet it felt: the video was playing on a laptop, which had been filmed by a phone camera. Of course, it turned out I’d been watching a bootleg, and that extra frame wasn’t part of the original.

Recent findings suggest that dawud’s film Palcorecore (2024) can be read in Jafa’s lineage. Like Jafa, Dawud cuts together found footage in an act of memory, love, and grief. The footage shows Palestinians flying kites, breakdancing, rapping, riding horses, and playing by the sea. Children surround a tank; a mute man desperately mimes a murder he witnessed. “The internet exists to document its own martyrdom,” a computerized voice indicates, playing on the fact that the Arabic word for martyr comes from the root meaning “to witness.” “We are martyrs together,” the voice says: we are witnesses together.“What interests me about internet cinema is that it creates a history of internet artists, the thoughts and languages they develop online, and the possibility of establishing a continuity between what they produce on the internet and how it can be given a temporal form through cinema,” wrote Dawud in an email. “Internet cinema doesn’t merely document an existing culture; it participates in the creation of its history. It is a way for the internet to historicize itself.”Ultimately, internet cinema is less a practice than a name: one that gives form to a whole range of ways of making online that are often lost in the tumult of the internet’s incessant production. If there is one thing that separates the art world from online cultural production, it is that the art world is nothing if not a form of memory. In its obsession with provenance, catalogues, and archives, it is a network of stewardship. Internet cinema is a means of making an object of what is so fleeting online, by turning the internet into a film.

What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns.
  • It has been revealed that each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build.
  • Whether you’re in the throes of a newly introduced romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

It has been revealed that each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a newly introduced romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

In a recent development, from those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:.

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

It has been revealed that research highlights that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

In a recent development, if the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

In a recent development, hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

Shigeru Ban unveils proposal for tent-like church in Rome

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The church will occupy a currently underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects.

A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.

The church will occupy a currently underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban’s signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.

According to Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci, the overarching goal is for the church to help establish a greater sense of community and place in the area, which they describe as having a “fragmented urban fabric”.

“We wanted to design a place of worship that also brings the whole community together,” remarked Ban.

“The timber structure expresses the idea of a tent, a simple, welcoming form that connects people with one another and with their surroundings. Through this project, we hope architecture can help create a new sense of belonging in the neighbourhood.”.

Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci’s proposal was the winning entry of a competition for the church.

It is one of five winning designs selected as part of the New Churches Programme – an initiative led by the local church district, the Diocese of Rome, and the Italian Episcopal Conference, an assembly of Catholic bishops, to provide permanent homes for parish communities in the region.

As part of the project, four upcoming churches will be built, while one existing parish complex will be extended.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be built on a raised public plaza, with various parish facilities, community spaces and a priest’s residence embedded below.

Its key feature will be its angular roof, which is shaped like a cross but not immediately readable as one. This is modelled on a latent cross – a feature in sacred architecture, in which a cross shape is integrated in the spatial design, without being clearly visible.

It has been revealed that inside, the church will have a diamond-shaped strategy, with large stained-glass windows positioned in the four cardinal directions. They will be triangular in shape and feature designs modelled on neighbourhood street art.

The project will be complete with a landscaped park, as well as various recreational and sports facilities, which the studios said will “create opportunities for social interaction and everyday activities”.

According to recent reports, the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex is not the first church project by Ban. Among his others is the landmark Cardboard Cathedral in Upcoming Zealand, which is formed of 98 cardboard tubes combined with wood and polycarbonate. We named it the most significant building of 2013 in our list of the 25 most significant buildings of the 21st century.

Other Italian church proposals recently featured on Dezeen include Stefano Boeri Architetti’s design for the Ambrosian Monastery in Milan, which will have a sail-like roof form.

Images courtesy of Shigeru Ban Architects.

#114523. Warhol’s Watches

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1788 w)

Warhol’s Watches

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Piaget’s second collaboration with The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts translates the pop artist’s 1986 Camouflage self-portraits into dials made of gemstone marquetry.
  • Recent findings suggest that one brand, however, stood out.
  • It has been revealed that housed in an 18-karat gold, 45 mm cushion-shaped case designed by Jean-Claude Gueit, Piaget’s then artistic director, the striking piece, which was part of a limited series manufactured between 1972 and 1977, featured a black onyx dial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Piaget’s second collaboration with The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts translates the pop artist’s 1986 Camouflage self-portraits into dials made of gemstone marquetry.

Recent findings suggest that one brand, however, stood out. Warhol owned at least seven wristwatches by the Swiss maison, Piaget. Founded in 1874 in La Côte-aux-Fées, a village in the heart of Switzerland’s Jura mountain range, the house was renowned in the latter half of the 20th century for its creative selection of timepieces in unusual shapes, many featuring dials made of exotic ornamental stones. One of those watches, a quartz-powered reference 15102 model that Warhol purchased from the brand in 1973, now forms the foundation for a Piaget collection bound to appeal to lovers of art in general and fans of Warhol’s revolutionary oeuvre in particular.

It has been revealed that housed in an 18-karat gold, 45 mm cushion-shaped case designed by Jean-Claude Gueit, Piaget’s then artistic director, the striking piece, which was part of a limited series manufactured between 1972 and 1977, featured a black onyx dial. Fittingly, it was called the Black Tie. In 1988, Piaget purchased Warhol’s watch at Sotheby’s landmark sale.

The artist’s choice of Piaget was no accident. In the 1950s and ’60s, the house had built its reputation on extreme thinness, introducing ultra-thin movements that transformed the watches into slim, supple pieces of jewelry. By the 1960s, Piaget had paired that technical prowess with a bolder sensibility: gold bracelets, vivid hardstone dials, and silhouettes that owed more to the jeweler’s bench than to the watchmaker’s. The result was a crossover brand that suited the decade’s appetite for spectacle. For Warhol, who drew no line between commerce and art, a watch that doubled as a gem-set object was irresistible. The Black Tie’s onyx dial, as sleek and dark as a lacquered cigarette case, could not have been better suited to the man who documented the era’s elite so closely.

Industry observers note that twenty-six years after Piaget purchased the Black Tie, the brand used the occasion of its 140th anniversary in 2014 to create a revival collection called Black Tie Vintage. The line caused such a stir among Piaget’s clientele that in 2024, for its sesquicentennial, the maison decided to up the ante. Thanks to a collaboration with The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Piaget was given the rights to rename the Black Tie Vintage watch after Warhol himself.

It has been revealed that the first collaborative watch to emerge from Piaget’s work with the foundation was the 2025 Collage, a limited edition of 50 pieces featuring an artful composition of ornamental stones—yellow Namibian serpentine, pink opal, and green chrysoprase—inspired by Warhol’s Polaroids. This month, Piaget has introduced a second piece, which also uses ornamental stone marquetry, this time to pay tribute to the Camouflage self-portraits that Warhol created in 1986.

“When you buy it, you don’t only buy a watch, you buy a whole story and heritage,” Jean-Bernard Forot, Piaget’s head of patrimony, tells ARTnews. “You can, of course, talk about the material, what it does for you. But at the same time, you have to talk about Warhol, you have to talk about Piaget, you have to talk about art.”.

Limited to 86 pieces, after the year in which Warhol created the eight-print Camouflage series, the watch, whose dial combines the ornamental stones sodalite and turquoise with satin-finished yellow gold and polished rose gold, faithfully interprets the artist’s work without blindly mimicking it.

“Camouflage is very difficult to work on, even in design, because we don’t just copy and paste the artwork—we have to find another way to express camouflage,” Forot notes.

Among the final serial group of paintings Warhol completed before his untimely death in 1987, the works paid homage to the military-inspired camouflage pattern, originally intended to help soldiers blend in with their surroundings. In Warhol’s hands, they became a comment on Abstract Expressionism, not to mention a deeply personal statement on his lifelong effort to conceal his true self beneath wigs, makeup, and a carefully constructed facade.

Industry observers note that printed in acid brights across enormous canvases, the swirling forms feature in self-portraits overlayed with Warhol’s face, framed by his signature shock of hair. For an artist who spent his life hiding in plain sight, the Camouflage series is arguably his most meta work.

Sources indicate that in order to capture the essence of the paintings on the face of a watch, Piaget’s artisans took some liberties with color. Rather than emphasizing Warhol’s use of yellow, for example, they highlighted the brand’s use of turquoise, Forot notes.

Recent findings suggest that “Once the team finished the drawing, which was validated by The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, then they started working with the gem material,” he notes. “We have to try to remain true to both the design itself as well as the techniques.”.

Study the dial of the watch and you’ll see something of an optical illusion: a sense of depth and texture that isn’t quite there. “When you look at the Piaget Camouflage, you have the feeling that you have four layers,” Forot notes. “But in fact, it’s an illusion because they are all flat and on the same level. Even if you have the feeling that the turquoise is above the gold, in fact, it’s at the same level.”.

The careful craftsmanship required to make the watch—each dial features 27 pieces of gold and ornamental stone marquetry and takes more than 100 hours of labor to design, research, and craft—is a testament to Piaget’s decades of expertise in the esoteric world of gem-setting. Since the maison introduced gold and color into its watches in the 1960s, it has worked with some 50 different ornamental stones, including lapis lazuli, jade, coral, onyx, and tiger’s eye.

The maison’s legitimacy in the realm of color is unassailable—and enduring. Piaget designated 2026 its “Year of Color,” based on its Colours of Extraleganza collection, representing the third and final chapter of a high jewelry trilogy that began with the maison’s 150th anniversary in 2024. “Piaget is really coming back to visibility in color and gold,” Forot says.

While the blend of hues on the dial of the Camouflage watch lends the piece its name and raison d’être, don’t overlook its iconic gold frame nor the movement that ticks within. The cushion-shaped case features three rows of textured grooves known as gadroons, a Piaget signature. It houses a self-winding manufacture movement, the 501 P1. And let’s not forget the caseback, where Andy Warhol’s signature appears alongside the number of timepieces in the limited series.

Best of all, the Camouflage limited edition, like the Collage that came before it, is steeped in the lore that swirls around Warhol’s personal history with Piaget.

Sources indicate that “Warhol was a real collector—of everything,” Forot indicates. “But even if he owned many watches from many brands—including Patek Philippe, Cartier, Bulgari, and so on—there is only one picture with him and the founder of a watchmaking company. And it’s Yves Piaget.”.

It has been revealed that the legendary chairman of the maison, Yves Piaget is the fourth generation of his family to be involved in the business, which was founded by Georges-Édouard Piaget in 1874 and acquired by the Swiss luxury group Richemont in 1988. In the 1970s, at the height of the brand’s 20th-century popularity, Yves and Warhol became friends.

It has been revealed that A photo of the men dated 1979 offers proof that they found common ground in their shared love of timepieces. At the time, Yves presided over the Piaget Society, a glamorous social circle centered on the brand and its community of jet-setting movers and shakers. And Warhol, of course, had the Factory, his studio in Manhattan, a hub of art, filmmaking, and creativity.

In a recent development, “They weren’t exactly the same, but they were both surrounded by artists, extravagant personalities—they were social long before The Social Network,” Forot claims. “In a sense, they had the same philosophy.”.

Yves’ recollections of Warhol during that time paint the artist as a quiet figure, whose later fame didn’t square with his penchant for careful observation.

Nevertheless, the two hit it off. Yves invited Warhol to Palm Beach to attend the world cup of polo, a sport that the maison made famous through its 1979 Polo timepiece, an emblem of the rich and famous. And he continued to send Warhol gifts, including boxes of chocolate, that the artist, a true magpie, kept as part of his time capsules. Stored in cardboard boxes, the objects, ephemera, letters, and gifts Warhol collected included personal relics from his multiyear friendship with Yves, although Forot jokes that the box of chocolate, while part of the collection housed by The Andy Warhol Museum in Pittsburgh, is, thankfully, empty.

In a recent development, warhol’s attraction to the brand was hardly anomalous. Piaget’s clientele included more than its fair share of the rich and famous, including Jackie O, Elizabeth Taylor, and Halston. Even Salvador Dalí was a longtime collaborator. In 1967 the surrealist teamed with Piaget on a collaborative collection of gold watches and jewelry, long before such partnerships became commonplace. Featuring gold coins, dubbed Dali D’Or, emblazoned with profile portraits of himself and his wife, Gala, the watches and jewels that emerged from the partnership offer yet another testament to Piaget’s high-flying reputation as the watch for those in the know and a symbol of wealth, taste, and extravagance, all qualities that continue to define the brand today.

Michael Dayton Hermann, managing director of strategic initiatives at The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, says that the collaboration with Piaget “is an expression of how the artist’s vision remains as relevant and compelling today as ever.”.

“This unique ongoing project is especially meaningful given Warhol’s personal friendship with Yves Piaget and his passion for the maison’s watches, which he collected during his lifetime,” Hermann tells ARTnews. “It also embodies Warhol’s belief in the creative possibilities of art and commerce, generating proceeds that support the foundation’s philanthropic mission, which has awarded more than $300 million in grants to advance contemporary visual art.”.

Just as the collaboration celebrates Warhol’s singular take on the role art plays in commerce, it equally underscores Piaget’s decades-old legitimacy in the world of art. Watches may not be the first things that come to mind when recalling Warhol and his legacy, but he collected them, wore them, and, in the case of Piaget, befriended the man who made them. Think of the Camouflage limited edition less as a commercial arrangement and more as the next chapter of a decades-long conversation started by Warhol and carried on in gold and gems.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

According to recent reports, these machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:.

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he claims.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study highlighted that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe notes this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he claims.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe claims. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”.

Sources indicate that nobbe indicates WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

Meet Swedish Girls, Sabine Marcelis’s pick for Dezeen's 20x20 project

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1247 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler.
  • The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.
  • “I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sabine Marcelis has nominated Swedish Girls as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project sponsored by Kohler. In this interview, we learn why the design duo deliberately play into stereotypes.

The steady emergence of Swedish Girls has not been lost on prolific Dutch designer Marcelis, who nominated the collective as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design over the next 20 years.

“I really like how they work with existing industrial production processes, yet the result very much speaks to the current culture,” Marcelis told Dezeen, explaining her selection.

Josefin Zachrisson and Mira Bergh run multidisciplinary studio Swedish Girls between Stockholm and Milan, creating furniture, installations and set design.

The duo met during their studies at Sweden’s Beckmans College of Design, where they graduated in 2019. They bonded over a desire to make work “without hierarchies” and maintain creative control of the studio’s output, which they prefer to call their ever-expanding “universe”.

The Substantial Bang for Swedish Girls was the selection of their collective’s tongue-in-cheek name, chosen after their first exhibition outing at Milan design week.

For experimental platform Alcova in 2021, Zachrisson and Bergh unveiled their ongoing metal rod Seats System project (pictured left).

Originally a single piece of modular seating without a defined front or back, the project has evolved into more metal pieces that follow the same design language, including a fruit bowl and a candle holder.

Industry observers note that “We overheard people talking about our furniture, asking who made it, and others were like, ‘ah, it was those Swedish girls’, and we felt a bit belittled by it,” recalled Zachrisson. The duo had previously made work under their own names.

“The Swedish girl has obviously become a phenomenon,” added Bergh. “You know, blonde, sexy. But when we were talking about it, we also found it really funny because it’s so stereotypical. We thought we’d call ourselves Swedish Girls because everybody else was already calling us that.”.

Humour is intrinsic to Zachrisson and Bergh’s interdisciplinary practice. Even their website, admired by Marcelis, was playfully designed as a Swedish Girls-branded Google search engine. It is meant to look like the internet itself, complete with mock web pages listing each of the collective’s projects.

“We got the idea when we rolled out the name Swedish Girls,” the pair explained.

“A professor from Beckmans called and said that we should change our name because when she Googled ‘Swedish Girls’, the search result was not exactly art and design,” they added.

“We thought that was so funny and decided to make Google about us instead of changing our name.”.

Another of the duo’s wit-inflected projects is Only Fans, an installation presented at Gothenburg’s Röhsska design museum in 2024 during local music festival Way Out West.

Dubbed “a multidimensional art experience about fan culture” in all its forms, the installation included 25 electric fans, selected as a riff on adult content platform OnlyFans, where women are often the subject of scrutiny.

“The installation was interactive, so that visitors could stand in the middle of the fans in a hysterical storm,” noted Bergh.

Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things. But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life.

Alongside the fans, the collective presented seven laser-cut steel chairs emblazoned with I <3 Swedish Girls, along with a fanzine and female mannequins wearing “metal merch” designed by Zachrisson and Bergh.

“Our work is a lot of these really silly, stupid things,” considered Zachrisson.

Sources indicate that “But it’s also layered with some seriousness, because the projects handle things that we are affected by and women are affected by in real life,” she continued. “It feels like a way to approach it that makes it accessible.”.

It has been revealed that “Sometimes it’s hard because we get these questions like, ‘are you a feminist?'” added the designer. “But it’s inherently political to be a woman moving through the world. Our work is just reacting to our reality.”.

The pair is keen to highlight that although they make furniture, “social values are always a starting point” for their projects.

“We really want to have a practice that feels purposeful,” said Zachrisson, considering the significance of partnering with institutions like design museums.

“We’ve realised that showing work in public spaces is the most notable thing,” she continued.

“Especially because the materials and processes we use have become quite expensive. So we want to put our pieces in public spaces so that everyone can take part in some way.”.

“You meet all different kinds of people, and we talk to them and grow from it,” added Bergh.

It has been revealed that the hardest thing is to earn money. We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money.

Despite Swedish Girls’ various collaborations and recurring presence at Milan design week, seven years after leaving Beckmans, Bergh and Zachrisson continue to work in cafes and supermarkets to fund their design practice.

The duo are hyperaware of the difficulties faced by emerging creatives, especially those like themselves who, as they put it, “want to listen to your gut and be close to the process”.

Sources indicate that “The hardest thing is to earn money,” said Bergh. “We’re adults, we’ve been doing this a long time. But we are still taken advantage of and expected to work for free or for very little money on very quick timelines. I feel like we should have more respect.”.

It has been revealed that “You don’t get paid in a way where you as two people can survive,” added Zachrisson. “But all these years of working and keeping our creative integrity is paying off in every way except financially.”.

When it comes to building their studio, the designers consider themselves to be playing the long game.

“Long term, it’s an investment to do it this way because we have now created a context where we can feel freedom and gain respect, which is why we were so happy when Sabine nominated us,” said Zachrisson.

“You can measure success in so many different ways and with this we feel respected, and that is so valuable.”.

The duo said funding that they won from Sweden’s Konstnärsnämnden arts council after graduating gave them a significant leg up when they were just starting out.

Zachrisson and Bergh are concerned that scholarships like theirs have been scarcer across Sweden in recent years thanks to the country’s right-wing administration, which came into power in 2022 and has only just been voted out of office.

According to recent reports, “All the artists we have talked to have felt an extreme difference in that time,” noted Zachrisson. “The share of the total budget allocated to culture has not been this low in 26 years.”.

Still, the pair are confident and excited about what’s to come.

According to recent reports, “It comes in handy that we have a broad practice,” stated Bergh. “We have intends for the future to make it easier for ourselves to be designers.”.

Industry observers note that “I like how they surprise with their projects and feel like we have only seen chapter one of their story,” concluded Marcelis. “And I can’t wait to discover the next chapter.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The new London Museum has been a humongous undertaking: 10 years in the making, costing £437 million in total against a budget of £337 million, and yet, after all that time and money, it’s hard to know where any of it went.

Recent findings suggest that from 1976 to 2022, the city’s museum, then called the Museum of London, occupied a site on London Wall at next to the Barbican complex. It moved to Farringdon, a grittier neighbor of the City’s financial district, because the old building was hard for visitors to find and too small to display the full collection. Related Articles Bloomberg Donates 14,000 Artifacts Unearthed in Renovation to London Museum Warhol's Watches.

The upcoming space is bright and airy, closer to an Erewhon café than a museum lobby. An on-site café, open around the clock from Thursday to Sunday, serves hot chocolate and ginger beer. The furnishings, though, feel random in such a pristine setting: a flock of large plastic sheep meant for sitting on, and shop signs from London fixtures like the Odeon cinema and Morley’s, the fried chicken chain. When was the last time any Londoner saw a sheep in the city? In theory, all of this should appeal to Londoners who have taken up early-morning run clubs, traded pints for matcha lattes and aren’t above a gimmicky bit of decor.

“People are looking for community, and they will have it in the museum,” Sharon Ament, the museum’s director, told ARTnews.

The architects, Asif Khan and Stanton Williams, working with the conservation specialists Julian Harrap Architects, have designed a space that’s inviting.

Industry observers note that “It took people until the 21st century to realize that cultural institutions are for everyone, and that’s what we strive to make here,” Khan told ARTnews at the press preview. He wants visitors to dip in and out of the story of London without feeling as if they’re in a museum. “When we look at audiences outside of the regular museum visitors, many find it challenging and don’t feel welcome. This is a welcome for those people,” Khan said. Entry is free, there are three separate entrances, and built-in sofas with reading lights invite passersby to stop in, though few people pass through Farringdon unless they’re waiting for the nightclub Fabric or the cocktail bar Space Talk to open.

According to recent reports, still, London is a city of 9.1 million people and a global center for art, film, music, finance and fashion. Finding stories that capture its quirks shouldn’t be that hard.

In a recent development, the museum is divided into three sections. Real Time, at the main entrance, represents London today and includes Banksy’s Piranhas sentry box. (What could be more London than Banksy?) In the Linbury Hall, Our Time attempts to tie the city together through objects like the Lord Mayor’s State Coach from 1757, the Buckingham Palace switchboard and Syd’s Coffee Stall, an East End food cart that operated from 1919 to 2019. Downstairs is Past Time, perhaps the only part of the museum that feels like a museum. It’s the most educational section, with small rooms on the women’s suffrage movement and the Great Fire of London. The rest of the floor is scattered with a piece of a fatberg, Tom Daley’s diving trunks from the London 2012 Olympics, a chair owned by Charles Dickens, a 2,000-year-old Roman wall painting, Anna Pavlova’s tutu for The Dying Swan and more.

The London Museum is a work in progress and until it figures out what sets it apart from the city’s other museums, it will remain a large crèche, where parents can bring their children to roam freely. But there’s still some hope: in 2028, the museum will open two temporary exhibition spaces, perhaps the museum will finally lean into its London-ness and celebrate the cornerstones that makes the city so glamorous and gritty, from the Teddy Boys of 1950s, Mods and Rockers of the 1960s to the Sloane Rangers of the late 1970s and 1980s.

It has been revealed that until the London Museum gets it right, the city has the Bayeux Tapestry, on view at the British Museum through July 11, 2027, with tickets topping out at £33 ($44). At the preview, word went around that one journalist had skipped it in favor of the 950-year-old cloth. In hindsight, I should have done the same, or stayed home to play Grand Theft Auto VI.

Industry News: Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

📅 30 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets.
  • According to recent reports, protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant!
  • And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

According to recent reports, protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

Recent findings suggest that so, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are substantial, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:.

It has been revealed that don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Sources indicate that keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

It has been revealed that sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Sources indicate that variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

Sources indicate that what you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

According to recent reports, introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!
