#114384. Latest Update: Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1704 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For more than a decade, buildings bearing trees have been sprouting up all over the world, from Upcoming York to Paris to Shanghai to Sydney.
  • It has arguably become one of the defining architectural trends of our era, taken up enthusiastically by top studios including BIG, MVRDV, MAD and Ateliers Jean Nouvel.
  • Almost every time Dezeen publishes an arboreal structure, a volley of comments crying greenwashing and gimmickry soon follows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Main photo by Dimitar Harizanov.

For more than a decade, buildings bearing trees have been sprouting up all over the world, from Upcoming York to Paris to Shanghai to Sydney.

It has arguably become one of the defining architectural trends of our era, taken up enthusiastically by top studios including BIG, MVRDV, MAD and Ateliers Jean Nouvel.

And yet, not everyone is a fan. Almost every time Dezeen publishes an arboreal structure, a volley of comments crying greenwashing and gimmickry soon follows.

Sources indicate that so, are the haters right on this one? Or do the arguments stack up in favour of wooded buildings?

To proponents of the approach, some of the benefits of putting trees on buildings are indisputable.

“I’m totally in favor of not only trees on buildings, but any type of natural habitats on buildings wherever it’s possible,” stated Fernando Scherner, an associate director in the nature and biodiversity team at engineering firm Buro Happold. “There are a few things that I think we can’t even argue about anymore.”.

In a recent development, there is, Scherner told Dezeen, strong evidence that vegetation on buildings bolsters biodiversity. And, he states, “there’s no discussion” that done right, shade and evapotranspiration from leaves can effectively keep homes cooler in hot weather, reducing the need for air conditioning – and therefore energy use.

But this second point gestures towards the crux of the debate about trees on buildings.

Such buildings require extra structural material to support the weight of the trees and soil, increasing the carbon cost by more than what the trees themselves will be able to sequester. Critics therefore argue that any carbon savings from reduced energy use are a red herring, because a similar benefit could be achieved through much simpler passive cooling measures such as awnings and shutters.

“I think that criticism is entirely legitimate, particularly if carbon sequestration is being used as the main justification,” said World Green Building Council technical lead for sustainable buildings Carolina Montano Owen.

“Trees do sequester carbon, but relatively slowly compared with the upfront emissions that can arise from additional reinforced concrete or steel needed for large planters, supporting structure and associated systems.”.

Even Dutch architecture studio MVRDV, one of the most fervent incorporators of trees on buildings, admitted in its Carbon Confessions exhibition held earlier this year that it would take hundreds of years to offset the climate impact of its La Serre project in Paris, right now under construction. MVRDV declined to contribute to this article.

While the phenomenon of trees on buildings goes back hundreds of years, to the Guinigi Tower in Tuscany, the undisputed poster child for the current movement stands at the other end of Italy.

Bosco Verticale in Milan is a pair of residential high-rises covered in 21,000 plants, including 800 trees up to 20 metres tall. It caused a sensation upon its completion in 2014, and was later selected by Dezeen as that year’s most significant building in the world.

The architect behind Bosco Verticale, Stefano Boeri, has since delivered other “vertical forests” in Eindhoven, Huanggang, Tirana and Utrecht, with several more on the way.

As you’d expect, he is bullish about the benefits of putting trees on buildings. He points to analysis by Arup, which concluded that the embodied carbon of Bosco Verticale is just one per cent greater than a comparable building with balconies of the same depth without vegetation.

“The load of the greenery, including the soil, trees and so on, really only slightly exceeds the variable loads that, in any case, must necessarily be taken into account in the structural design of cantilevered space,” he told Dezeen.

Boeri argues that changes to the construction process – such as the use of prefabrication methods or mass timber – promise to cut the embodied cost further in future vertical forest projects.

Even so, Philip Oldfield, head of the University of New South Wales’ School of Built Environment, is not convinced.

“I think the equation is pretty challenging to make the case that trees on buildings are beneficial from a greenhouse-gas emissions perspective,” he told Dezeen.

However, Oldfield points out, that’s not to say that architects adorning their buildings with trees are necessarily acting in bad faith.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m a fan of Bosco Verticale,” he said. “I think it’s a really inspiring building, but not from a carbon perspective.”.

“What inspires me about Bosco Verticale is it notes, ‘hey, look: you can have a hint of suburban lifestyle in a high-rise urban building,’ which could make high-density living more attractive to a greater socio-economic spectrum, and then that may be more sustainable in the long run.”.

Though harder to measure than carbon, it’s generally acknowledged that incorporating greenery into dense urban settings has positives for human wellbeing.

For instance, when Oldfield helped to conduct a post-occupancy study of the social housing development Pinnacle@Duxton in Singapore, he witnessed children sitting under trees to do their homework 50 storeys in the sky.

“Singapore’s been able to add trees and green across its built environment, and it has fundamentally changed the experience of the city, I think for the better,” he mentioned.

With a very high-rise urban landscape, year-round hot weather, lots of rain and low wind speeds, Singapore is the perfect setting for buildings bearing trees, and the construction industry here has become adept at making it work.

But in other parts of the world, things have gone less successfully. Jean Nouvel’s One Central Park in Sydney, for example, had to undergo emergency repairs after one of its heavy planter boxes fell to the ground in 2022.

And in Chengdu, there were reports that barely any of the 826 apartments at Qiyi City Forest Garden were occupied a few years after its completion due to a mosquito infestation.

Even the most ardent fans of trees on buildings agree that it’s not always the right solution.

“I’m totally positive about it, but I think it should be taken case-by-case,” mentioned Scherner. “There may be cases where the purpose or the objective of the project are not really realistic.”.

“If the right multidisciplinary team is not there from the start – and I’m talking about ecologists, horticulturalists, together with engineers, structural engineers, architects, landscape architects and all that – then many things can go wrong.”.

Recent findings suggest that “There are many flops,” remarked Boeri. “If you decide to follow the approach that we have, you take several risks, so it’s very crucial to be aware of the risk and to run all the technical challenges and tools that you need if you want to do it properly.”.

“Botany is not a superficial discipline – it’s very complex, very rich, and so when you want to realise a building where trees are acting as live subjects, you have to study a lot.”.

Bosco Verticale was subject to a huge amount of strategic planning in collaboration with botanists, from the selection and preparation of the plants, to soil chemistry, to developing systems for irrigation and maintenance.

According to recent reports, “Flying gardeners” now scale the buildings twice a year, while thousands of ladybirds were purchased to control pests and cranes were installed on top of the towers in anticipation of removing larger dead trees. In the event, Boeri claims fewer than 15 trees have died at Bosco Verticale, and the cranes have never been required.

Sceptics’ early predictions of mass plant deaths at buildings bearing trees have, in general, not come to pass.

But concern about whether some of these buildings are more interested in making a visual statement than being ecologically responsible has lingered.

For Montano Owen, this is the crucial test of whether the approach is justified.

“The difference is whether planting is an integrated environmental strategy or primarily aesthetic,” she said.

“A poor example is essentially decorative: oversized concrete or steel planters added to achieve a ‘green’ aesthetic, substantial additional structural loads, high irrigation requirements, inappropriate species, difficult maintenance access and high tree mortality.”.

Boeri agrees. “I believe that what we have done works because we were not considering plants as an ornamental presence, and this is very vital for me,” he remarked. “What we are doing is really to create buildings for trees, a house for trees.”.

Among the most high-profile projects accused of using trees as mere decoration is Heatherwick Studio’s 1,000 Trees shopping centre in Shanghai, completed in 2022.

Soon after the finished building was unveiled, Oldfield criticised the design in a piece on Dezeen.

“The trees are a one-liner, contributing to a sense of urban drama, but with little substance as to how they might provide tangible benefits to the environment, or the community,” he wrote.

Subject to similar criticisms recently was MVRDV’s design for the upcoming Rotterdam Rocks!. Writing on Dezeen, architecture historian Barnabas Calder called for the project to be scrapped, saying that “putting plants on a building doesn’t make it sustainable, any more than dropping a basil leaf on a steak makes it vegan”.

These studios may argue – as Heatherwick Studio leader Thomas Heatherwick has previously done – that there is intrinsic value in designing buildings that capture the imagination of the public.

That in turn feeds into a broader debate about whether the priority for architecture should be to minimise up-front carbon, or maximise the chance that buildings are retained by future generations.

In any case, with the trees-on-buildings trend showing little sign of abating, Montano Owen has a checklist for architects taking up the approach.

According to recent reports, “Start with the local context and environmental needs,” she noted. “Choose species that are suited to the location. Minimise extra structure, materials and loads. Consider water and maintenance needs from the start. Strategy for vegetation to survive, grow and mature long term. Avoid solutions that need heavy structures, intensive irrigation or frequent plant replacement for limited environmental benefit.”.

In a recent development, “The key question is this,” she added. “Is this the best place and most resource-efficient way to achieve the environmental benefits we want? Sometimes trees on buildings could make sense. In most cases, trees at street or ground level may provide greater benefits with fewer resources.”.

In a recent development, to limit the toll of El Niño's October-December rains, IGAD's specialized climate institution, the Climate Prediction and Applications Centre (ICPAC), has released a practical guide with UN-Habitat for Horn of Africa cities. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) is a regional bloc in Eastern Africa of governments from the Greater Horn of Africa, and their High-Level Call to Action on El Niño Preparedness establishes a regional commitment to move from reactive disaster response to proactive action for long-term resilience. Emphasizing cross-border coordination and crediting local knowledge, the call states: "We recognize that climate and disaster risks do not respect national borders, and that no single country or institution can manage them alone.".

In the eastern Horn, a 90% probability of above-normal rain is projected to deliver up to 70% of the entire year's rainfall in just three months, swinging dry landscapes violently from drought to deluge. In contrast, Uganda and the Lake Victoria Basin are growing wetter, with October-December seasonal totals exceeding 400mm – a probable 6-13% increase over average OND rains in some parts and 25% or more in others, triggering urban floods and highland landslides.

Industry observers note that at the national policy level, the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) secures anticipatory governance through The Uganda Roadmap on Anticipatory Action (2026-2031). It was developed in collaboration with government ministries, such as the Ministry of Water and Environment; agencies, including the Uganda National Department of Meteorological Services, district local governments; civil society organizations; academic institutions, namely Makerere University, and development partners, including WFP, FAO, ICPAC, URCS, UNDRR, the World Bank, IOM, Save the Children and others. Formulated around six strategic pillars, the framework aims to strengthen Early Warning, develop standardized Anticipatory Action protocols, integrate those into national Policies and Advocacies, improve Governance and institutional Coordination, secure sustainable Financing Mechanisms, and strengthen Monitoring, Evaluation, Research and Learning.

Within its own jurisdiction, KCCA, which is recognized as a UNDRR Making Cities Resilient 2030 Resilience Hub, ramped up clearing operations across 69 critical flood blackspots following August 2026 El Niño warnings. Kampala's stormwater network stretches 212 kilometers of primary and secondary channels alongside 700 kilometers of tertiary and community drains, creating a combined system nearly long enough to stretch from Kampala to Mombasa, Kenya. So far, KCCA has serviced about a quarter of its main network, across major arteries including Lubigi and Nalukolongo, as well as upgrading other channels under the KCRRP. Sources indicate that beyond clearing, KCCA continues to caution against improper waste disposal that clogs waterways, pairing public recommendations with daily sweeping across 401 roads and periodic cleanings on 54 others, and a weekly Weyonje community clean-up drive. Long-term, the city is shifting towards sorting, recycling and reusing via a planned Material Resource Recovery Facility at Buyala. Moreover, since flood management is compounded by encroached wetland buffers, preparing safe havens and community hubs ahead of moderate or severe rains is crucial. Because human life comes first, OPM early-warnings guide towards evacuating flood-prone wetlands and lowlands, which reorganizes informal economies that activate street edges as well as informal housing. However, that safeguard creates another vulnerability: if relocation is not handled properly, clearing the spaces that sustain affordable living and vital street commerce risks cutting residents off from their daily livelihood. Yet still, there is a practice in finding middle ground.

Participants agreed on four action pathways, including: integrating local council leaders and community waste collectors into service governance, regular desilting of drainage reserves, expanding household recycling, building local participation and mobilizing Village Health Teams. Industry observers note that state authorities, humanitarian actors and multi-agency technical services have debuted coordinated preventative operations in Djibouti City since 2024. Most notable is the four-year Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems (CREWs) Djibouti initiative, involving the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR), Djibouti Red Crescent Society (DRCS) and Conoscenza e Innovazione (K&I) to strengthen capacity for response to hazards such as flash floods and landslides. At the national level, the project has modernized forecasting and helped the forthcoming National Framework for Climate Services (2026-2030). Locally, it established Community-Based Early Warning Systems featuring hazard mapping, first aid training and a national community flood management reference guide.

A May 2026 WMO mission included a full-scale flood simulation drill in the capital's Vietnam neighborhood, expanding community outreach to ensure alerts reach high-risk groups, including the elderly, women, children and persons with disabilities. At the institutional and technical level, and ahead of the anticipated El Niño -driven rainfall, the National Office for Water and Sanitation (ONEAD), Rural Development Agency (ADR), Roads Office (OVD) and local sub-prefectures focused on clearing invasive prosopis trees, construction debris and solid waste from stormwater drainage networks across vulnerable areas such as Cité Progrès in the Third District. Building on these infrastructure efforts after an ICPAC forecast predicted 50- 100 mm rainfall for mid-October, the Djibouti Red Crescent National Society activated its Simplified Early Action Protocol to protect 2,500 vulnerable residents in the flood-prone Boulaos area through early warning outreach, drainage clearing, sandbagging shelters, roof reinforcement, water treatment, and evacuation support.

Sources indicate that the UN-Habitat and ICPAC guide aligns closely with Djibouti City's call to pair forecasts with quantifying triggers and neighborhood mobilization. It demonstrates the value of locally grounded urban action based on regional climate intelligence. While Kampala must manage excess water across its saturated landscape, arid Djibouti faces a hydrological paradox of retaining scarce water while defending against torrential onslaught. Lasting resilience depends on deeper water harvesting, aquifer recharge systems, desalination, and resilient drainage infrastructure. Together, the two cities illustrate that anticipatory governance ought to extend beyond forecasting towards addressing underlying infrastructure gaps and spatial inequalities that sustain urban vulnerability.

Industry observers note that "My entire architecture is based on windows. Windows completely adapted to the new conditions of reinforced concrete and metallurgy, but also readapted to human functions. Windows are of paramount concern."—Le Corbusier.

According to recent reports, "My entire architecture is based on windows. Windows completely adapted to the latest conditions of reinforced concrete and metallurgy, but also readapted to human functions. Windows are of paramount concern."—Le Corbusier.

Indeed, in shaping a building envelope, windows regulate the relationship between interior and exterior, frame views, allow natural light and ventilation to enter, and contribute to thermal and acoustic comfort. However, two windows with similar dimensions, materials, and visual characteristics can deliver different performance levels once installed. Their effectiveness depends not only on the frame, but also on the type of glazing, the opening system, the hardware, exposure conditions, and how each component connects to its surrounding environment.

Recent findings suggest that specifying a window involves more than simply choosing an aluminum profile that meets an aesthetic intent. It requires understanding how technical variables interact and determining which combination of properties best suits the building's location, orientation, use, and environmental conditions. A system designed for a residential opening in a relatively protected environment, for example, may not be the most appropriate solution for a large glazed facade exposed to strong winds, heavy rain, or urban noise. Every enclosure system must be understood and adapted to its surrounding environment.

Industry observers note that specifying a window involves more than simply choosing an aluminum profile that meets an aesthetic intent. It requires understanding how technical variables interact and determining which combination of properties best suits the building's location, orientation, use, and environmental conditions. A system designed for a residential opening in a relatively protected environment, for example, may not be the most appropriate solution for a large glazed facade exposed to strong winds, heavy rain, or urban noise. Every enclosure system must be understood and adapted to its surrounding environment.

Yet, beyond the availability of systems, common errors continue to impact the specification process. One of the most frequent is prioritizing thermal insulation while overlooking acoustic performance, water tightness, air permeability, wind resistance, solar control, safety, and durability. Furthermore, glass is often treated as a secondary component, even though its composition can significantly influence the overall performance of the enclosure. Choosing glazing without considering the frame's capacity, solar orientation, outdoor noise levels, or safety requirements can compromise the effectiveness of an otherwise adequate system.

In a recent development, moreover, a window's performance is intrinsically linked to its size, proportions, number of sashes, and operating mechanism. Larger openings carry different structural demands, influence hardware selection, and may require specific reinforcements or alternative configurations. Similarly, sliding and hinged systems offer different sealing solutions and operational characteristics that must be considered during the design phase. Installation must not be underestimated either. Even a high-performance window can lose much of its effectiveness if the joint between the frame and the surrounding wall is poorly resolved. Thermal bridges, inadequate sealing, a lack of insulation continuity, or poorly executed drainage details can compromise the performance levels verified in laboratory tests.

Comparisons, Relationships, and Performance.

When comparing window systems, the overall performance of the assembly is influenced by frame depth, sash dimensions, the configuration of the thermal break, and the capacity to accommodate different glazing compositions. In aluminum windows, the thermal break typically consists of polyamide strips that separate the inner and outer sections of the frame, thereby reducing heat transfer through the metal. Its dimensions, geometry, and integration with other insulating materials determine the profile's thermal performance.

In aluminum windows, the thermal break typically consists of polyamide strips that separate the inner and outer sections of the frame, thereby reducing heat transfer through the metal. Its dimensions, geometry, and integration with other insulating materials determine the profile's thermal performance.

Recent findings suggest that the STRUGAL S64RP GALA, S74RP OPTIMA, and S82RP AURA systems illustrate different approaches to meeting these requirements. With frame depths of 64, 74, and 82 mm, respectively, these systems incorporate various profile configurations and insulation strategies. While GALA offers a relatively compact solution with reinforced insulation options using polyamide and optional polyolefin foams, OPTIMA incorporates tubular polyamides in the sashes, providing high thermal performance even in demanding climate zones. AURA takes thermal insulation to the next level through the use of 42 mm polyamide strips, a cellular EPDM center gasket, and passive insulating foams, offering optimal performance even in the harshest weather conditions.

Their differences are also reflected in their glazing capacities. STRUGAL S64RP GALA accommodates glass thicknesses of up to 51 mm in the visible sash, STRUGAL S74RP OPTIMA reaches up to 61 mm, and STRUGAL S82RP AURA supports glazing up to 69 mm. These variations allow for a wider range of double- or triple-glazing configurations, depending on the project's requirements for thermal and acoustic insulation, solar control, and security.

While thermal transmittance is typically one of the first values considered during specification, air permeability, water tightness, wind resistance, and acoustic insulation are also vital aspects of a window's performance. For example, water tightness, evaluated under the UNE-EN 12208 standard, measures resistance to water penetration. The STRUGAL S74RP OPTIMA system achieves class E2400, whereas STRUGAL S82RP AURA and STRUGAL S64RP GALA reach E2100, and STRUGAL S88RP ARTIS features a 7A rating. In terms of acoustic performance, the certified values range from Rw ≤ 42 dB for STRUGAL S88RP ARTIS to Rw ≤ 47 dB for STRUGAL S82RP AURA.

How Project Requirements Dictate System Selection.

In a recent development, in real-world projects, the selection process becomes clearer when observing the convergence of technical requirements, architectural intent, and environmental conditions. Its 64 mm frame, relatively compact profile, and reinforced insulation options illustrate how window replacement can adapt to the constraints of a pre-existing facade. #114381. Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

📅 18 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1076 w)

Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

📅 18 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1076 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people.
  • In a recent development, in fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb.
  • If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

In a recent development, in fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” notes Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller states, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, says Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

Industry observers note that at the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

Industry observers note that an allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.).

Recent findings suggest that by contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran states. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

Sources indicate that if you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication before pollen counts rise. That's because antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

Industry observers note that both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller states. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.).

It has been revealed that the less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

It has been revealed that whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller says to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

It has been revealed that if the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran claims. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Sources indicate that nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she says.

Sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller claims. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

If you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

This year Simon Skinner was named emerging designer of the year at the Dezeen Awards. Here, he selects five projects that showcase his work.

Swedish designer Skinner set up his studio in 2020 and has rapidly become known for his sculptural furniture and installations that explore rethinking and reusing found materials.

“My practice is centred around material culture, exploring the relationship between objects, meaning and everyday life,” Skinner told Dezeen.

“What connects my work is an interest in how forms carry associations and how these can be reshaped to offer latest perspectives on things we know and take for granted.”.

Skinner finds that the things that excite him about design are also “the same things that make me suffer”.

“You never quite know what’s coming next when running your own practice, but there’s also something exciting about that uncertainty,” he remarked.

“A material or an object you’ve overlooked for years can suddenly become the starting point for a whole body of work.”.

Over the coming year, along with creating new collections and public installations, Skinner hopes to dedicate more time to research.

“I want to make more room for research and experimentation, and give myself time to follow an interest before knowing exactly where it might lead,” he said.

Sources indicate that “When I started researching Afro combs at Konstfack, I became aware of how much history and symbolism an everyday tool can hold. That experience still informs how I work,” he continued.

“I want to keep exploring the objects and forms we take for granted, looking at the meanings they’ve inherited and what happens when you change their material, scale or context.”.

Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning Skinner, as described by the designer:.

“An ongoing project in which vintage glass sourced from flea markets and second-hand shops is brought together in sculptural lighting compositions.

“Drawing on the memories and associations embedded in these found objects, the work explores the relationship between material, memory and light.”.

“Crafted in my studio, these combs celebrate rituals and traditions surrounding textured hair.

“Informed by historical references and personal experiences, they reimagine an everyday object through distinctive forms and symbols.”.

“Extending the exploration of beauty rituals within the Syntax collection, the Vanity Table offers an alternative reading of an object associated with personal grooming.”.

“These one-of-a-kind pieces, a daybed and an armchair, are upholstered in hand-dyed canvas in deep magenta hues.

“Combining traditional upholstery techniques with an experimental approach to colour and detail, the pieces embrace the irregularities of the dyeing process, making them an integral part of their character.”.

It has been revealed that “This piece of furniture explores our relationship to the mechanical lock. The lock is integrated into the leg, with keys used to secure the connection between the leg and the seat.

“The keys can also serve as hooks for keychains and personal belongings, inviting individual expression.”.

Industry observers note that london Museum opens in its new home in West Smithfield's restored General Market on Saturday, November 28. The institution, formerly known as the Museum of London, closed its previous location at 150 London Wall, near the Barbican complex, on December 4, 2022. The relocation project has taken a decade to bring the collections representing the city's story, from the prehistoric inhabitants who settled by the Thames to today's global city, to a newly restored historic building. Stanton Williams led the transformation of the General Market, with collaborating architect Asif Khan Studio and conservation architects Julian Harrap Architects. London Museum opens in its newly introduced home in West Smithfield's restored General Market on Saturday, November 28. The institution, formerly known as the Museum of London, closed its previous location at 150 London Wall, near the Barbican complex, on December 4, 2022. According to Director Sharon Ament, the project is a collective endeavor that tells "the city's story in all its grit and glitter.".

Industry observers note that the Museum is organized into three main spaces. Real Time is the main entrance, a covered former street known as West Poultry Avenue, where animated screens display data about London in the moment, from the number of pubs and bees to Londoners' changing moods. Visitors will find Banksy's Piranhas sentry box here, as well as a clock tower with the last bell cast at the Whitechapel Bell Foundry, which will ring the Museum open each day. At the center of the building, Our Time occupies the former trading floor of the General Market, known as the Linbury Hall. A restaurant, a shop and a show space for families and schools surround 13 large installations, including the 1757 Lord Mayor's State Coach and the Buckingham Palace switchboard, on display for the first time. Syd's Coffee Stall will serve free hot drinks every Tuesday.

It includes five focus galleries, among them Votes for Women, and a six-meter window overlooking Thameslink trains that pass between Farringdon and City Thameslink. Highlights include the Cheapside Hoard, Roman writing tablets from the Bloomberg Collection and the Bowes Cup, displayed for the first time. The permanent galleries are free to enter. The Museum is open Sunday to Thursday from 10 am to 6 pm, and Friday and Saturday from 10 am to 11 pm, with last ticketed entry at 7:15 pm on those late nights.

A rotating culinary residency, The Roost, opens in early 2027, the same year as the free exhibition Londinium: the making of a Roman city, scheduled for spring in the 800-square-meter underground vaults. The adjacent Poultry Market will follow in 2028 with two temporary exhibition spaces, a learning center and a collection store. The £437 million project returns the General Market to public use for the first time in over three decades, and the City of London Corporation expects around two million visitors a year, which it links to its wider prepares for the Smithfield Barbican area.

According to recent reports, architect and designer Patricia Urquiola has chosen fellow multidisciplinary Laerke Ryom as her pick for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, Ryom discusses her innovative work and how it’s rooted in Danish design traditions.

Ryom, who is based in Copenhagen, first came to many people’s attention as one of the co-founders of the design community Ukurant.

Together with fellow founders Josefine Krabbe Munck, Kamma Rosa Schytte and Kasper Kyster, Ryom indicated her work as part of its first exhibition at Danish design week 3 Days of Design in 2020, and Ukurant promptly became a recurring highlight of the design event.

Since graduating from the Royal Academy of Fine Art in Copenhagen’s master’s program in furniture and object in 2022, Ryom’s tactile designs have continued to evolve, and she has worked with a range of materials and products.

For her collection Blå, she made handwoven denim upholstery out of worn-out jeans, while the Buckle chair, made with furniture brand Fredericia, resembles a leather jacket.

“I find very interesting the way she moves naturally between furniture and textiles, starting from discarded materials and giving them a latest logic through simple gestures,” Urquiola remarked of why she chose Ryom.

It has been revealed that “There is something light in the way she works. Her work feels open and still very much in evolution.”.

This experimentation has become something of a signature for Ryom, whose latest exhibition, Raiments, was a sleek exploration of how upholstery could almost become a furniture piece in itself.

To the designer, her work now is in some ways a continuation of the projects she worked on during her time at the Royal Academy.

“During my studies, I was investigating different materials and different typologies, which I actually still think I’m kind of doing – I don’t see myself as limited to one material,” Ryom told Dezeen.

While she “really strongly identifies as a furniture designer”, Ryom has also designed smaller products, such as metal bowls for the Bread & Butter exhibition in Copenhagen and quilted lamps.

To her, function is always at the forefront, and Ryom believes that even details that appear to be purely decorative have a function if they tell a story.

“Even when I’m doing collectible things for galleries, I’m always thinking of the functionality of the pieces,” she explained.

“Even if you can say, ‘[what’s functional] about doing a little skirt on a chair’, as on the Raiments chair, it tells a story; a story of the cover being loose, something that is its own thing, [separate] from the frame. For me, that’s still a function or a means to an end.”.

Her aim is to create pieces that straddle the line between collectible and functional design; something that is artistic and yet commercial enough to someday go into production.

“I want it to be something where the distance between the categories disappears, and they become a shared thing,” Ryom explained.

“That’s something I think a lot about, that the collectible design and the artistic work I do should have a little sprinkle of something that you could see in production.”.

The collectible design and artistic work I do should have a little sprinkle of something that you could see in production.

The idea of giving beauty to everyday objects, rather than creating pieces that are purely functional or purely aesthetic, is one that has deep roots in the Scandinavian design tradition.

While Ryom’s pieces might not be the pale-wood designs usually associated with Danish design – though she has worked in wood, using offcut wooden pieces to design furniture for Ukurant in 2023 – she sees herself as part of this tradition.

“Even if people don’t think that what I do looks like typical Danish design, I feel like it’s completely rooted and very fundamentally based on the principles of the Danish design tradition,” she explained.

“I view myself as someone who is not in opposition, but who is developing or following along [with it].”.

While her own pieces in the past have so far mostly been made in smaller quantities, Ryom sees positively on the current trend of big brands, such as IKEA and Disney, working with younger designers and mass-producing their work.

She believes it helps to spread knowledge about designers to a public that isn’t always aware of the people behind the products.

“I think it’s an vital thing because what we see, at least here in Denmark, is that the knowledge about designers today, for the general public, is crazy small for a nation that kind of brands itself as a design nation,” Ryom said.

“Talking to my parents, even with them having a designer for a daughter, they’re still trying to figure out ‘what is it that you actually do’?

Inspiration can only take you so far – at some point you need to get working on it, interpret it and experiment with it.

Ryom herself, meanwhile, says she sees a big difference between her current work and that of a few years ago. She thinks it comes from “starting to believe in yourself and your intuition, and getting more skilled in your craft”.

But, she also consciously works on developing her ideas and taking them from the initial inspiration stage to the final product.

“Inspiration is something that I stumble upon in my everyday life, but at the same time, it only becomes interesting when I sit down and work with it,” she said.

“Inspiration can only take you so far – at some point you need to get working on it, interpret it and experiment with it and investigate what the substance of the inspiration actually is.”.

As someone who’s constantly exploring upcoming materials and ways of designing, Ryom also highlights the importance of collaboration. She says that while she likes doing a lot of the work on her furniture herself, she has also gotten better at reaching out to experts to get input for some of her pieces, including her Enfold chair.

The steel chair is covered in a ruched leather upholstery, held in place by buttons, that creates a very tactile, sculptural seat.

“It did it all myself, but I reached out to a fashion designer who does a lot of leather bags, and I could talk to her and ask ‘how would you do the finishing here, or what kind of tool would you use there?'” she mentioned.“I really like figuring things out myself and doing it myself, but seeking the knowledge of those people who have really done the craft.”.

Being chosen by Urquiola meant a lot to Ryom, who really admires the Spanish designer.

“It was actually a little surreal, because she is someone that I look up to,” Ryom mentioned. “When you can say anyone in the world, I feel very, very honoured that she pointed at me – that’s a huge thing.”.

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

Can You Actually ‘Boost’ Your Metabolism?

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1440 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism.
  • Many of these supposed hacks don’t have much research backing them up, and the ones that do won’t meaningfully move the needle when it comes to your weight.
  • Recent findings suggest that metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism. It seems like just about everyone wants to “boost” or “speed up” their metabolism in the hopes of burning more calories and, as a result, losing body fat. In reality, this is not an easy task, but you wouldn’t know that from the countless TikToks claiming it’s as simple as taking a shot of apple cider vinegar, hopping into an infrared sauna, or braving a cold plunge.

The truth? Many of these supposed hacks don’t have much research backing them up, and the ones that do won’t meaningfully move the needle when it comes to your weight. Improving your metabolism actually boils down to a few basic tenets that aren’t flashy or sexy but can have long-term benefits for your overall health and well-being. We’ll get into all that, but first, a little background on what your metabolism even is.

Recent findings suggest that metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight. Having a “fast” metabolism means your body burns calories rapidly, making it easier to maintain or lose weight, while having a “slow” metabolism means you gain pounds more easily and have a harder time taking them off. This isn’t wrong, per se, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. Your metabolism is the way your body turns food into energy. This energy is then used to power your heart and lungs, build and repair tissue, regulate hormones, and perform other critical functions.

Put more succinctly, “metabolism is all the chemical processes that keep our body alive and functioning,” explains Jonathan Gabison, MD, an assistant professor of family medicine at the University of Michigan who is board-certified in obesity medicine.

For example, about 20% of the energy your metabolism provides goes to your brain, building neurotransmitters and keeping signals going, so having an efficient metabolism is critical for cognitive health.

In short, yes. Your metabolism is influenced by loads of factors, from genetics and age to weight. But that doesn’t mean your metabolism is fixed. It’s actually highly modifiable, says Shebani Sethi, MD, a clinical associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and the founding director of the world’s first academic metabolic psychiatry clinical program.

Industry observers note that that said, taking shots of apple cider vinegar in the morning or picking up “metabolism-boosting” supplements won’t do the trick. Research demonstrates that improving your metabolism requires consistent long-term habits. Here are five that can make an impact.

Every time you move your body, it burns calories and raises your metabolism—both during the moment and for a period afterward. Think of your metabolism like a pie: Two thirds of the energy you use every day is devoted to keeping you alive (that’s your basal metabolic rate), and the rest goes toward digesting food and moving your body. Being more active is the most straightforward way to up your metabolism. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.

According to recent reports, this can include dedicated exercise, like a jog, hike, or workout class. (The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.) But it also extends to all the movement you do outside of formal exercise, known as NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis). Increasing your daily step count, prioritizing physical hobbies like gardening and walking your dog, or even taking on more household chores and grocery runs all count toward upping your overall movement.

According to recent reports, strength training helps build and maintain muscle mass. Muscle tissue is metabolically active, which means sustaining it burns more calories than maintaining fat tissue. Therefore, having more muscle mass will give your metabolism a slight boost.

By strength training you’re also improving your overall health. For instance, since muscle tissue uses the majority of the glucose in your bloodstream, more muscle mass can increase your body’s capacity to use glucose and help prevent blood sugar spikes. Plus, research has shown that having more muscle helps improve insulin sensitivity, including in individuals without diabetes.

According to recent reports, those same CDC exercise guidelines suggest including at least two days of strength training every week. That can include body-weight moves like push-ups and lunges; lifting weights with dumbbells, kettlebells, barbells, or cable machines; or utilizing resistance bands. Dr. Gabison says what’s most vital is being consistent with your exercise routine, so it’s best to choose workouts you’re likely to stick with. And remember, if you’re just starting out, it’s important not to push yourself too hard early on and risk injury.

In a recent development, protein is having a major moment right now. While things may be getting a little out of hand (hello, protein popcorn), consuming sufficient amounts of high-quality protein has well-established benefits for your metabolism. That’s because the nutrient is the building block of muscle, so eating enough of it helps support muscle growth and maintenance, especially if you’re resistance training.

Protein also has the highest thermic effect of all three macronutrients, meaning digesting it burns more calories than carbohydrates or fats. Plus, it’s the most satiating macro, so increasing your protein intake can help you feel fuller and fend off cravings, which may help with weight management.

However, balance is key. Sun Kim, MD, MS, a board-certified endocrinologist and associate professor of medicine at Stanford, says doctors and health care providers have different viewpoints on how much protein is enough for optimal health. In her opinion, “most Americans eat plenty of protein without trying,” she says, cautioning that consuming excessive amounts won’t magically speed up your metabolism and could even worsen insulin sensitivity in some cases. So unless you’re extremely active, there’s no need to get hundreds of grams a day.

Industry observers note that for most healthy adults, the recommended dietary allowance for protein is 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day. That means a 120-pound person needs roughly 43 grams of protein a day, which is about what you’d find in two four-ounce hamburger patties. If you incorporate some protein into every snack and meal throughout the day, you should easily hit the mark. That said, some groups need more. People who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or highly active may need up to 2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. Older adults and those taking GLP-1s should also be mindful of their intake, as reduced appetite can lead to inadequate protein intake and muscle loss, particularly when coupled with reduced physical activity.

Industry observers note that an often-overlooked habit for better metabolism is getting quality sleep. A lack of sleep dysregulates your metabolism, causing a cascade of complications, including worsened glucose management, more intense hunger the next day, and reduced energy expenditure. (Sleepy people are less likely to move their bodies.) When this happens consistently, it can lead to an increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Sleep also has an impact on hormones that can slow down the metabolism.

There isn’t a specific number of hours you should sleep each night, but research indicates that most adults do best with seven to nine hours of quality rest most evenings.

Sources indicate that prolonged stress keeps your cortisol (stress hormone) levels chronically elevated, which can break down muscle tissue and slow your metabolism. Constantly pulling out your hair can also disrupt your appetite-regulating hormones, triggering cravings that may prompt you to eat more. All of these things can affect your weight. Research shows chronic stress can increase your risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and related cardiometabolic complications too.

There is, sadly, no quick fix for reducing stress, so some trial and error might be required to figure out what works best for you. Some places to start are doing yoga, meditating, practicing breathing exercises, going for walks outside, journaling, spending time with loved ones, engaging in relaxing hobbies, or starting therapy to talk through whatever is weighing on you.

Sure, supporting a healthy metabolism can increase the number of calories you burn and help with weight management. But it can also improve what’s known as your metabolic health, which encompasses measures such as blood pressure, cholesterol, insulin sensitivity, and total body fat. Having good metabolic health is essential for preventing chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease. The healthier your metabolism, the more calories you burn and the better your metabolic health.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Fran Mart.

London architecture practice Tuckey Design Studio has renovated and extended Bay House in rural Yorkshire, using a rich, moody palette intended to evoke the feeling of a wine bar.

The project involved reconfiguring and expanding the country house dating from the early 2000s, while introducing a garden spa and sauna.

Tuckey Design Studio was tasked by the clients to recreate the feeling of their favourite wine bar, which informed a palette of dark timber carpentry, terracotta-painted walls and a bespoke wine storage cabinet alongside a tasting area.

“The ambition was clear from the beginning: to bring the atmosphere of a much-loved London wine bar into the home,” project lead Fraser Biggins told Dezeen.

“The clients’ enthusiasm for wine and music became important touchstones for the design, informing both the arrangement of the spaces and the character of the interiors,” he added.

The home’s previously cramped interiors are now centred on a large, double-height atrium, which serves as both a point of arrival and a gathering and tasting space with a bespoke timber “wine wall”.

This hall is finished with dark timber panelling, terrazzo floors and terracotta paintwork, with a wall alongside an arched composite stone staircase punctured by small square openings.

This central space leads through into the social spaces, with a kitchen and dining space finished using similar dark timber panelling and concrete countertops.

According to recent reports, the stairs lead up to the first floor via a landing with a built-in bench, where a balcony connecting the bedrooms enjoys views of the hall below. It also looks across the garden through windows in a latest bay window extension.

“The central hall forms the organising principle of the house, providing a shared space from which the surrounding family rooms and activities unfold,” Biggins told Dezeen.

“A series of interconnected spaces, galleries and overlooking balconies create visual connections across different levels, allowing the house to feel both connected and varied,” he added.

On the first floor, two of the existing bedrooms have been converted into a games room and bar space, finished in dark shades of green and grey.

Alongside them are four ensuite bedrooms finished in warmer shades of pale pink and yellow, with each featuring a hand-painted mural designed to “reflect the character of each occupant”.

“Material choices were guided by a desire for honesty, durability and longevity,” Biggins told Dezeen.

“We wanted the spaces to feel timeless and comfortable, without relying too heavily on traditional materials or references.”.

“Instead, the palette brings together robust, tactile finishes that feel natural and lived-in, allowing the character of the materials to speak for themselves,” he added.

The exterior of the extension has been finished in composite stone and dark accoya wood, and looks across the home’s garden to the standalone spa and sauna, which was designed as a “complementary counterpoint” to the main home.

Previous projects by Tuckey Design Studio include a home in Wiltshire constructed using walls of unstabilised rammed earth and a residence within a converted chapel in Devon.

The third edition of the Sharjah Architecture Triennial (SAT03), titled Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures, brings together practitioners exploring architecture beyond conventional building practices. During the opening week, ArchDaily's Editor-in-Chief Christele Harrouk spoke with Makram el Kadi and Ziad Jamaleddine of L.E.FT, Mohamad Nahleh, Khondaker Hasibul Kabir and Suhailey Farzana of POCAA, May al-Ibrashy of Megawra-BEC, Nathalie Harb and Mohamad Hafeda, and Hamed Bukhamseen and Ali İsmail Karimi of Civil Architecture about their contributions, which engage with spiritual practices, community-led spatial production, heritage, displacement, and material reuse. Through installations, collective research, and interventions in existing spaces, their work considers how architecture can emerge through different forms of knowledge, care, and engagement with everyday life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, certain influencers have built entire social media empires out of making everything from scratch. Oftentimes, their videos carry an implicit sense of moral superiority, suggesting that you’re not a good parent (or at least not as good as them) if you’re resorting to pre-packaged store-bought items. Those who pick their own produce and painstakingly hand-craft their own candy necklaces simply work harder, love their children more, are fundamentally better.

Recent findings suggest that but this suggestion is hardly fair. For the vast majority of people—meaning those who don’t make their living off of wellness content or have near-endless amounts of time and money to burn—canned, frozen, and packaged stuff is almost always a far more practical option. “Groceries are a fortune,” after all, Anthea Levi, MS, RD, a Brooklyn-based health writer and the founder of Alive+Well Nutrition, tells SELF—and fresh items tend to be the most expensive, as a trip to the produce section of the supermarket will readily prove.

It has been revealed that besides the lower price point, canned, frozen, and packaged foods have one other major advantage: their staying power. “You can keep them in your freezer for months, so that often gives people confidence” in the purchase, since they know they don’t have an expiration date hanging over their head, Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. This, in turn, leads to reduced food waste: “Fresh salad greens are notorious for going slimy in the fridge, but you’ll never have that matter with frozen spinach. Ditto for fish. Fresh fish needs to be cooked ASAP before it turns, while frozen fish and canned or tinned fish last until you’re ready to use them,” Levi claims.

Industry observers note that nielsen also takes concern with the basic idea that these options are somehow inherently inferior—“a significant, big misconception,” in her eyes. “There has been a lot of confusion about the nature of these foods in general. Just because something is processed or packaged does not mean it’s unhealthy,” she says.

Industry observers note that in other words, canned, frozen, or packaged items are often perfectly fine to include in your diet—and you shouldn’t feel embarrassed, ashamed, or inadequate if they make frequent appearances in your meals (or if they’re your first resort over fresh). “Constant access to fresh foods is, unfortunately, a luxury. If canned, frozen, or packaged items are the only way you’re able to put a fruit or vegetable on your plate, go for it,” Levi says. But if you’re still concerned about the health aspect, there are a few key ways to maximize the nutritional value and improve the overall experience. Here’s what to know to make the most of your freezer stash.

“Typically, the fewer ingredients, the better,” Levi claims—a rule of thumb to consider while shopping. While canned, frozen, and packaged items have a reputation for being ultra-processed—rife with additives and lower in nutritional value—there are actually plenty out there “that are made from just one or two whole-food ingredients, such as canned peas, frozen fruit, and canned salmon,” Levi says. “These are as close to fresh foods as you can get, and just as nutritious.” Many jarred peanut butters only contain dry roasted peanuts and salt, for example. (By contrast, Ritz peanut butter crackers, which have an ingredients list several rows long, are a very different story.).

It has been revealed that that said, this glitch can be nuanced. “Just because an ingredient looks fancy or technical or like a chemical does not necessarily mean that it's bad for you,” Nielsen points out. Many processed foods—including bread, milk, and breakfast cereal—are fortified with healthy vitamins and minerals that you might not otherwise consume enough of in your diet. Take vitamin C—which may appear under the name “ascorbic acid”—as an example. “You might not recognize that what you’re looking at is vitamin C, so you don't want to scare yourself off of potentially nutritious and valuable food because you see things on the ingredients label that you don't recognize,” Nielsen indicates.

Sources indicate that in Nielsen’s experience, canned foods are often considered even less “healthy” than frozen, but the stigma isn’t necessarily warranted. Canned beans, which boast fiber, plant-based protein, and minerals like iron and zinc, are an excellent example of a canned food that amounts to an “incredible nutrition source,” she notes. Still, this category does have one major drawback: Staples like veggies, soups, and, yes, beans can contain a significant amount of sodium, a mineral that can cause high blood pressure and related issues like heart disease and stroke when overconsumed. Tinned fish like TikTok’s beloved sardines can suffer from the same matter, as the brine inside the tin can be heavy on added salt as well.

Given that many brands offer sodium-sensitive alternatives, try to prioritize those options instead to keep your sodium intake in check and avoid potential health consequences, according to Nielsen. Look for labels like “No salt added,” “Low sodium,” or even “No sodium” to steer you in the right direction. If you can’t find anything fitting that bill at your local store, draining and rinsing canned products before use can also drastically cut down on the sodium content—by up to 40%, according to some estimates. (Just keep in mind this method may also cause losses in other nutrients, like vitamin C.).

Recent findings suggest that “In terms of packaged and processed foods, I'm always looking for a couple of nutrients to minimize and a couple of nutrients to optimize,” Nielsen says. Sodium is one to limit or avoid, as we’ve already covered, but there are others too—like added sugars and saturated fat. “Peaches that come canned in sugary syrup aren’t as nutritious as peaches that come canned in water, or are purchased frozen or fresh,” for example, Levi says.

According to recent reports, on the other hand, when you’re reading over a nutrition facts label, “what you want to see is fiber,” Nielsen notes—and “protein is a massive bonus.” Multiple vitamins and minerals in a product is also often a positive sign. Even breakfast cereals, which are often thought of as unhealthy, “can be incredible sources of minerals like iron and zinc—things that we need that help to keep our metabolism running, that keep us energized,” Nielsen says.

Recent findings suggest that trying to decide between two (or more) similar products? Comparing and contrasting the ingredients can help you narrow it down, according to Nielsen. Take breakfast cereal: You’ll want to ask yourself, “‘Which one of these cereals gives me the most fiber, the most protein, has the least sugar?’” she says. In this case, the relative content of vitamins and minerals can also be a helpful clue. Seeing that a cereal contains 10% to 20% of your recommended dietary allowance, as many do, can be “your sort of gut check that this is actually a really nutritious food,” Nielsen says.

Sources indicate that even though frozen veggies are affordable and durable, they do have one significant downside compared to fresh: Their taste and texture can take a hit—and, in turn, “you do have to adjust your cooking somewhat,” Nielsen says. To prevent sogginess, cook frozen veggies from frozen rather than letting them defrost first, according to Levi. And you’ll want to use heat-based cooking methods (like air-frying, baking, roasting, and stir-frying) “as opposed to water-based methods like boiling or steaming,” she says.

According to recent reports, “Many of us are working more than ever before—maybe working two or three jobs—and we don't have a lot of time to put a home-cooked meal on the table,” Nielsen says. Strategically pairing your canned, frozen, and packaged items is an easy way to boost efficiency in the kitchen without sacrificing nutritional value. If you’re having canned soup for dinner, you can dump in a can of lentils to boost the fiber and protein, for example. (Bonus tip: You can also use this approach to stretch out your leftovers. Need a batch of spaghetti to last longer? Toss some frozen peas on top or some frozen broccoli on the side.).

Recent findings suggest that “Stocking your freezer and pantry with budget-friendly canned, frozen, and packaged items can help make balanced meals a breeze,” Levi notes. Follow the tried-and-true “plate method” to guarantee a nutritious result, according to Nielsen: Reserve a quarter of your plate for whole grains or starchy vegetables, another quarter for protein, and the remaining half for fruits and non-starchy veggies. You could make rolled oats with chia seeds, frozen berries, and peanut butter for breakfast, or pasta with tinned sardines and frozen broccoli for dinner, for example, Levi says. “It sounds way too simple, but it is backed by so much science to help you balance your diet without counting anything,” Nielsen says. “As long as you stick to that plate method, you will be eating a nourishing diet”—yes, even if your ingredients don’t come to you direct.

Tech Report: Desai Chia designs Bethesda Residence to balance "openness and discretion"

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A large light well brings daylight deep into this private home that was designed by Desai Chia Architecture for a tight site in a dense Maryland neighbourhood.
  • The project takes its name from its location in Bethesda, a city located northwest of Washington DC.
  • The house is set within a suburban neighbourhood near the downtown district, where residential lots are about one-fifth of an acre (647 square metres).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Jake Balston.

A large light well brings daylight deep into this private home that was designed by Desai Chia Architecture for a tight site in a dense Maryland neighbourhood.

The project takes its name from its location in Bethesda, a city located northwest of Washington DC.

The house is set within a suburban neighbourhood near the downtown district, where residential lots are about one-fifth of an acre (647 square metres). Because the houses here are close together, the architects needed to be very mindful of privacy concerns.

“The clients sought a house that would feel open and light-filled without sacrificing privacy,” stated New York-based Desai Chia Architecture.

“Its compact lot and the close proximity of neighbouring houses required a careful response balancing both openness and discretion.”.

The architects intended the house to “rethink suburban-urban hybrid living through a modern lens”.

Industry observers note that roughly rectangular in initiative, it has three levels and a basement. Setbacks help break up the mass, particularly on the street-facing elevation.

The building appears “as a two-storey building from several vantage points,” the team noted.

“The home is carefully scaled to blend with neighbouring houses, balancing a strong architectural identity with sensitivity to its suburban context,” the team mentioned.

Facades are clad in grey fibre-cement panels made to last for a century. The material is known for protecting against fire, pests and extreme weather, according to the team.

“A durable, low-maintenance exterior with a strong architectural presence was a key client priority from the outset,” the architects said.

“Glass-fibre-reinforced concrete (GRFC) panels were selected to create a crisp, sculptural facade that captures texture and shifting light throughout the day.”.

A modern-style bay window adds dimension and visual interest to the front and back facades.

Within the home, public spaces are located on the ground level. The rear portion opens into a yard with a lap pool.

The upper levels contain bedrooms and two offices, and the top floor has a rooftop terrace. The basement holds a gym, ping-pong area and media room.

A limited number of windows helps ensure privacy. To provide natural illumination, the team created a three-storey light well, which is positioned along a central staircase and brings daylight deep into the dwelling.

“This vertical, faceted volume allows sunlight to cascade downward, distributing diffuse light from a small skylight across circulation spaces on multiple levels while minimising solar heat gain,” Desai Chia Architecture remarked.

It has been revealed that the all-electric house has a geothermal heating and cooling system. To enable the homeowners to age in place, the house has a shaft where an ADA-compliant elevator could be added in the future.

The homeowners are physicians, one of whom can walk to his practice in downtown Bethesda.

“When needed, the dedicated home offices allow both physicians to work from home in spaces with calming natural light,” the studio stated.

“Its location – easily walkable to downtown amenities and robust public transit – supports a connected pattern of work and family life.”.

Other homes in Maryland include a restored carriage house by Colleen Healey Architecture that features colourful facade panels and a family home by Ziger Snead clad in stone shingles, charred wood and weathering steel.

Design architect: Desai Chia ArchitectureArchitect of record: Thomson & Cooke Architects.

Buildner confirms the results of The Next House: USA, an international architecture ideas competition exploring how the familiar American suburban home might respond to changing household needs, affordability challenges, and environmental concerns. The competition invited participants to rethink the scale, layout, and construction of the single-family home, as well as its relationship with the surrounding neighborhood.

Buildner reveals the results of The Next House: USA, an international architecture ideas competition exploring how the familiar American suburban home might respond to changing household needs, affordability challenges, and environmental concerns. The competition invited participants to rethink the scale, layout, and construction of the single-family home, as well as its relationship with the surrounding neighborhood.

It has been revealed that the brief challenged architects and designers to propose a replicable housing prototype for a household consisting of two adults and one child. Rather than simply producing another suburban housing model, participants were encouraged to explore more efficient uses of space, flexible domestic arrangements, construction costs, long-term adaptability, and the potential for repeated housing units to foster a broader sense of community.

According to recent reports, the brief challenged architects and designers to propose a replicable housing prototype for a household consisting of two adults and one child. Rather than simply producing another suburban housing model, participants were encouraged to explore more efficient uses of space, flexible domestic arrangements, construction costs, long-term adaptability, and the potential for repeated housing units to foster a broader sense of community.

The selected proposals address these questions at different scales. Some retain recognizable residential forms while introducing compact floor intends, adaptable interiors, and off-site construction systems. Others reinterpret suburban land use through shared landscapes, clustered housing, additional dwellings, or the reuse of underutilized sites. Together, the projects explore the relationship between the individual home, the systems used to build it, and the broader environments in which it is replicated.

Sources indicate that following the first edition, Buildner has debuted The Next House: USA 2027, inviting architects, students, and designers worldwide to propose a new suburban housing prototype of up to 1,500 sq ft (approximately 140 m²). The new edition explores how a compact, adaptable home can be replicated across different American contexts, with winning teams receiving an invitation to compete for the €50,000 Buildner Medal.

Project title: Everyday HouseAuthors: Shengnan Gao, Telmen Bayasgalan, Penghui (henry) Zhang, United States.

Project title: Everyday HouseAuthors: Shengnan Gao, Telmen Bayasgalan, Penghui (henry) Zhang, United States.

Everyday House reinterprets the familiar pitched-roof American home through compact planning and a more open approach to suburban development. The project combines recognizable residential volumes with flexible living areas and integrated workspaces, allowing domestic functions to adapt within a restrained footprint. Prefabricated building components are considered alongside rainwater harvesting, solar energy, and passive environmental strategies. At the neighborhood scale, the houses are arranged within a shared landscape of gardens, productive planting areas, recreational spaces, and communal gathering areas, rather than following a rigid layout of isolated lots. The proposal preserves the identity of the conventional suburban house while exploring how its construction methods, environmental systems, and relationship with neighboring houses could support more diverse patterns of everyday life.

Project title: One Frame, Two HomesAuthors: Diego Rodriguez, France.

Project title: One Frame, Two HomesAuthors: Diego Rodriguez, France.

It has been revealed that one Frame, Two Homes explores a suburban dwelling organized around an independent structural framework that allows domestic arrangements to change over time. A steel skeleton is conceived separately from internal partitions and the exterior enclosure, enabling rooms and household configurations to be adjusted without altering the main structure. A larger greenhouse-like envelope creates intermediate spaces for planting, daylight, and seasonal use, linking the interiors with an inhabitable climatic buffer. The proposal also examines the subdivision and evolution of suburban lots, allowing both houses and surrounding parcels to adapt to changing needs. By separating the permanent structure from adaptable components, the design approaches the suburban home as an evolving framework rather than a fixed arrangement of rooms.

Project title: Common GroundAuthors: Chung Wei Lee, Yu Hsiang Lin, Buzz Wei, United States.

Project title: Common GroundAuthors: Chung Wei Lee, Yu Hsiang Lin, Buzz Wei, United States.

Common Ground proposes a compact housing system in which individual homes are arranged around shared outdoor spaces. Rather than dividing each suburban lot into entirely private front and backyards, the scheme pairs dwellings around communal gardens designed for planting, play, and everyday gatherings. The houses are based on a regular structural grid, with rotated interior layouts that establish varied relationships between rooms, terraces, and the surrounding landscape. Prefabricated components and a centralized service core support a repeatable construction approach, while alternative configurations ranging from one to four bedrooms allow the domestic program to adapt over time. By repeating the prototype, the proposal envisions a neighborhood defined as much by its shared green spaces as by its individual homes.
